title: LISTED: Architecting Large-Scale Classifieds and Marketplace Platforms
basis: Reconstructed after the fact from PLAN.md, config.yaml, the introduction, the three preface pages, the nine part introductions and the closing section of long-term-evolution. The journal level and every part are specified; posts are specified in full for the Preface only and at outline level elsewhere (folder, title and question taken from PLAN.md, case questions written from the case titles). Part theses for Parts I to IX are taken from each part introduction's key points and connection paragraph, not from a reading of every chapter, and need the author's confirmation.

know: How the systems behind a listing marketplace fit together as stages of one pipeline: listing model, supply, discovery, trust, money and the platform beneath them.
The fifteen named failure patterns and the liquidity metrics each stage protects.
believe: A listing marketplace is a liquidity machine, and its architecture is judged by how reliably it turns fresh, trustworthy supply into matches with demand.
In a marketplace group the most expensive problems sit at the boundaries between stages and between brands, and the hardest of them are problems of change, not of design.
can_do: Justify a freshness, latency or removal target by the liquidity metric it protects.
Locate a liquidity loss at a hand-off and name the contract, owner or metric that was missing.
Decide what a group should share and what each marketplace should own, and in what order to consolidate.
Go from the decision in front of them to the chapters that answer it.

audience.who: Experienced architects and engineering leaders working on listing marketplaces: chief and enterprise architects of marketplace groups, principal and staff engineers, search, data and ML leads, platform-engineering leads, product and engineering directors of classifieds, real-estate, automotive, jobs and recommerce marketplaces, and technology leaders integrating acquired marketplaces.
already_knows: What an API, a database, an event stream, a search engine and Kubernetes are.
How to make and defend an architecture decision.
does_not_know: Marketplace economics: liquidity, network effects, multi-homing.
Search and ML vocabulary: learning to rank, percolation, hybrid retrieval.
Regulatory detail: DSA statements of reasons, DAC7, P2B.
Vertical specifics: VINs, property and vehicle feed standards.

thesis.question: How should the systems behind a listing marketplace be designed, governed and evolved, especially in a group of many marketplaces, and by what measure should they be judged?
thesis.claim: A listing marketplace is a liquidity machine: listings, search, trust and monetization are stages of one pipeline whose throughput is liquidity, so its architecture should be judged by how reliably it turns fresh, trustworthy supply into matches with demand in every country, category and vertical while each marketplace evolves at its own pace; in a group that means sharing platforms beneath the brands, governed by published contracts rather than mandates, and changing them in the order that risks least liquidity, not the order that saves most.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a marketplace is a set of separate products (search, ads, trust and safety, payments), each optimized by its own team against its own metric, and that a group's platform is judged by synergy and run cost, so the goal of a group is one product on one stack.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this justifies every target by the liquidity metric it protects, spends design effort on the hand-offs between stages and between brands, caps every sale of attention against the match rate, and sequences each consolidation and migration by the liquidity metrics it puts at risk, accepting a slower saving to keep the match rate flat.
thesis.how_why: A marketplace rarely owns the goods or sets the price; what it provides is the probability that buyer and seller find each other in time, and that probability is local and compounds into network effects. Every stage can lose it: a slow publication, a sold item still advertised, a duplicate, a scam in the inbox, a paid placement that displaces a relevant result. Those losses sit between systems that each look healthy, and in a group, acquisitions and country launches multiply the boundaries.

supporting_claims.claim: A listing marketplace sells matches, and liquidity, local and compounding, is the measure every architectural choice should be judged by.

The business model and the vertical decide the architecture: where the marketplace's job ends sets identity, trust, payments and data, and sharing decisions rest on capabilities and bounded contexts, not on systems.
The listing is a small aggregate with one owner and a lifecycle that references governed, versioned reference data.
Supply arrives from systems the marketplace does not control, so it needs a contract per channel, provenance on every value and a publication path in which removal is faster than publication.
Every discovery surface is a read model of the listing stream, and the order of results is a policy with owners.
Trust and safety is a shared platform whose decisions every other stage must obey, and regulation asks for a few artifacts built once.
Every revenue line spends liquidity, so each sale of attention must be measured and capped against the match rate, and what was sold must be provably delivered.
A shared platform earns trust through published contracts, not mandates: share platforms beneath the brands, not products.
The hardest problems of a marketplace group are problems of change, sequenced by risk to liquidity and steered by fitness functions rather than toward a target state.
The public record of real marketplace groups supports these claims and shows where they stop applying.

additional_patterns.applies_to: part-2 to part-6: a listing followed through the machine in the order it moves, from model to supply, discovery, trust and money
part-7 to part-8: from the platform beneath every stage to keeping it coherent over time
part-9: the argument tested against the public record

flow.rationale: Part I's business vocabulary (model, liquidity cell, capability, bounded context) is what every later target and sharing decision is justified by, so it comes first. Parts II to VI follow a listing in the order it moves, so each part reads the output of the one before: discovery reads the supply Part III delivers, money sells the attention discovery creates. The platform comes after the stages because its contracts (the event stream, the register of copies, governed metrics) are defined by what the stages need; placed first, it would specify contracts for stages the reader has not met. Trust is not a stage a listing reaches after search; it acts at publication, on every discovery surface and in messaging. It comes after discovery because its decisions must reach every surface Parts III and IV built, and before money because messaging, where scams close, is where Part VI begins; placed before supply, it would govern surfaces the reader has not met. Change over time needs the platform it changes: consolidation, organization and migration move teams and brands onto contracts Part VII defines. Public cases come last because the reader needs the vocabulary and the patterns to read them critically; placed first, they would be anecdotes.

hook.content: At the end of a quarterly business review the general manager of a country's largest classifieds site shows contacts per live listing against a younger competitor with a third of the listings and more contacts per listing, and asks why; search availability was 99.95%, the moderation queue met its service level, feed imports were green every night and paid 'top listing' sales were up a fifth.

opening.bridge: From each team's green report to following one listing from the seller's first tap to the buyer's message, where the reasons sit at the hand-offs between systems.
opening.roadmap: This page gives the argument and how to read the book; the next page names the fifteen failure patterns; the third introduces Veldmark; Part I then begins with the business behind the listings.

closing.synthesis: Each part designs one stage of the liquidity machine; long-term-evolution maps each part to its stage, the guarantee that stage must give, the liquidity metric it protects and the failure pattern that appears when it does not, so the book's chapters read as one argument rather than nine topics.
closing.so_what: A group can measure every quarter, with marketplace fitness functions, whether its machine still turns fresh, trustworthy supply into matches, instead of steering by program milestones.
closing.callback: The introduction's central claim, restated in the same words, and its warning that the synthesis was left to this chapter.

takeaway.content: Steer the platform by a small set of marketplace fitness functions, each with an owner and a counter-metric, and test the argument against the public cases in Part IX.

non_goals.topic: Payments, the finance ledger and reconciliation in depth.
The internals of any real company beyond what it has published.

parts.title: Part I — MARKETPLACE: The Business Behind the Listings

know: The four marketplace models of the endpoint ladder and the six-axis marketplace profile.
Liquidity as matches per place-and-category cell, and the metric tree that measures it.
The industry's five waves and what each left in a group's systems.
Capability, value stream, heat map, bounded context, context map, published language, vertical requirement profile and the four-layer share test.
believe: In a listing marketplace the business model and the vertical decide the architecture, before any technology choice.
Duplication alone does not justify merging; what to share is decided on capabilities, contexts and vertical profiles, not on systems.
can_do: Describe their own group's marketplaces as profiles and liquidity cells.
Justify a freshness, latency or capacity target by the liquidity metric it protects.
Classify a capability part into shared platform, shared engine with vertical content, vertical capability with one owner, or brand product, and give the reason.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
A reader who has read only Part I can turn a 'merge the duplicates' proposal into a reviewable decision with the part's tools.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A group CFO proposes merging two brands' search systems and two brands' dealer-package catalogs because each is a duplicate. Using only Part I, what do you check before agreeing, and what is the likely answer?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Duplication alone proves nothing: score each capability separately for differentiation, maturity and duplication, and split it at level 3. Share the engine (search platform, catalog and entitlement service) and leave relevance and packages to each brand; check the vertical requirement profile, and move a vertical onto the shared engine only when the engine meets that profile.

thesis.question: What business is behind the listings, and why does it decide the architecture?
thesis.claim: A listing marketplace's architecture is decided by its business before its technology: where its job ends, per country and category, sets identity, trust, payments and data; liquidity, measured as matches per place-and-category cell, sets the systems' targets; and because a group's systems are sediment of past strategies and differ by brand while its capabilities mostly do not, what to share must be decided on capabilities, bounded contexts and vertical profiles: share the machinery, leave the content to each vertical, and keep every shared platform separable.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a marketplace group's architecture is chosen for technology fit and synergy, by picking the strongest brand's stack and consolidating every duplicated system onto it, with the business model and the vertical treated as product details on top.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this opens every platform debate with the marketplace profile register, the cell-level liquidity metrics, the capability heat map and the vertical requirement profiles rather than a systems inventory, and rejects a target or a merger that cannot name the business fact it serves.
thesis.how_why: The endpoint decides what the platform can observe and which regulators apply; liquidity is local, so national averages hide empty cells; a group's three search engines and four identity systems are fossils of launches, copies and acquisitions; and 'listing' means six different things to six teams. Systems therefore differ by brand while capabilities mostly do not, and verticals differ in physics that no category tree absorbs.

supporting_claims.claim: Where a marketplace's job ends (contact, lead, payment and delivery, or guaranteed outcome) decides its identity depth, bounded contexts, trust, data and regulation, and it varies per country and category, so it belongs in a configured profile, not a brand-wide assumption.
A marketplace sells liquidity, which is local to a place-and-category cell; measured as matches rather than inventory, its metrics set the platform's publication, alert, removal and capacity targets.
A group's architecture is the sediment of its corporate strategies, and because capital strategy changes faster than platforms, every shared platform must be separable.

Capabilities, not systems, are the unit for comparing brands, and scoring differentiation, maturity and duplication separately shows that duplication alone proves nothing: most answers split a capability into shared machinery and local content.
Boundaries go where the meaning of 'listing' changes: one context owns the listing's truth, and the others build their own views from a published listing event, never a shared table.

Verticals differ in physics, so a group shares the machinery, lets each vertical own its content on shared engines, gives vertical capabilities one owner, and moves a vertical onto a shared engine only when the engine meets its profile.

role.contribution: Supplies the business vocabulary (marketplace model, liquidity cell, capability, bounded context, vertical profile) that every later target and sharing decision is justified by.

flow.rationale: Each chapter uses what the one before established. The taxonomy comes first because liquidity is measured differently per rung (contacts, leads, outcomes), so the metric tree needs the endpoint ladder. History follows liquidity, not the other way round, because the chapter explains why groups are portfolios of local leaders by the local, winner-take-most network effects the liquidity chapter establishes; placed first, the five waves would be a chronicle without a cause. Capabilities follow history because history shows that a systems inventory is a record of past strategies and cannot be the unit for comparing brands. Placed before history, the capability map would read as a tidy-up of duplication rather than a correction of sediment, and its verdicts would lose the separability rule history adds. Bounded contexts need the capability map as input: Veldmark's 54 level-2 capabilities collapse into its 19 candidate contexts, and the heat map's verdicts split search into a platform context and brand relevance contexts. Vertical requirements come last because they ask where the sameness of the capability map and context map stops; before those maps, the share test's layers (shared engine with vertical content, vertical capability with one owner) would have nothing to classify. Ending on verticals also hands Part II the item identities and external systems of record its listing aggregate must leave room for.

hook.content: This book starts with the business, not the systems, because in a listing marketplace the business model decides the architecture: a classifieds site whose job ends at the contact, a portal that sells qualified leads and a marketplace that holds buyers' money need different identity, trust, payment and data systems, even when their search pages look alike.

opening.bridge: From the preface's group with four of almost everything to the three pieces of business knowledge any sharing decision needs: what kind of marketplace you run and what it sells, how the industry got here, and a description of the marketplace that outlives systems and reorganizations.
opening.roadmap: Six chapters as six questions in order: what kind of marketplace this is, what it sells and how to measure it, how today's groups formed, what the marketplace does independently of its systems, where the domain boundaries go, and what genuinely differs between verticals.

closing.synthesis: The model, liquidity, history, capabilities, contexts and vertical physics are one line of reasoning: together they say what every later design must respect before it chooses a technology, and they end in a share test that divides each capability into shared platform, shared engine with vertical content, vertical capability with one owner and brand product.
closing.so_what: Veldmark's architecture advice forum ratifies a shared-versus-specific table in April 2027 instead of 'four of everything', and Motorvane moves onto the shared ingestion engine only when the engine meets its own feed success rate and delete latency.
closing.callback: The part opening's claim that the business model decides the architecture and that capabilities, contexts and vertical profiles turn 'should this be one platform?' into a decision that can be reviewed; the closing chapter opens with exactly that question about four verticals.

takeaway.content: Before proposing a shared platform, write a numbered requirement profile for each vertical and place every capability part in one of the four layers with an owner and a reason; Part II then designs the listing inside those boundaries.

transition_in.introduces: The business before the systems: what kind of marketplace each part of Veldmark is, what it sells and how that decides the architecture.

thesis.question: What kind of marketplace is this, and why does the answer decide the architecture?
thesis.claim: A listing marketplace is defined less by what it lists than by where its job ends (at the contact, a qualified lead, a completed payment and delivery, or a guaranteed outcome), and each step down that ladder adds bounded contexts, data, identity checks, liabilities and regulators; because one brand holds several models across countries and categories, and marketplaces move along the ladder in both directions, the endpoint must be recorded per country and category as configuration, and every move toward the transaction treated as a category-gated bet with an exit plan.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the business model is a pricing and product choice layered on one marketplace platform, that each brand has one model, and that the industry is heading to transactions everywhere, so every brand should be built for payments now.

posts.title: Liquidity Is the Product: Network Effects, Local Markets and Marketplace Metrics
posts.question: What does a listing marketplace sell, and how do we measure whether it works?

know: Liquidity, cross-side and same-side network effects, multi-homing and disintermediation, and why the place-and-category cell is the unit.
The liquidity metric tree from fresh supply through exposure and contact to outcomes, with its counter-metrics.
believe: Liquidity metrics, defined carefully, are the source of most non-functional requirements in a listing platform.
can_do: Trace a publication, alert, removal or capacity target to the liquidity metric it protects, and reject one that cannot be traced.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two markets with the same buyers per listing and different outcomes, the reader says what to measure and which requirements follow.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Two countries have the same number of users per live listing, yet one gets far fewer contacts per new listing. Using only this chapter: what do you measure, and what engineering requirements could follow?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Split the data into cells (place × leaf category) and compare the share of liquid cells and of listings in them; measure matches (time to first contact, contact rate, sell-through) with counter-metrics, not listings or visits. Requirements follow from the metrics: publication and alert latency from time to first contact, removal speed from ghost share, and search capacity sized for the weekly peak from search-to-contact at peak.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Veldmark's Portugal-versus-Netherlands question; two-sided markets, network effects and the liquidity cell; competing for liquidity (seeding, winner-take-most, multi-homing, disintermediation); the metric tree; Veldmark's cell analysis; metrics turned into requirements; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes and the Chief Architect's view. Evidence: dated public sources and research, and fictional Veldmark figures.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: What does a listing marketplace sell, and how do we measure whether it works?
thesis.claim: A listing marketplace sells liquidity, the likelihood that a listing and a buyer find each other in a given place and category fast enough that both come back; because network effects work per place-and-category cell, national counts of listings and visits hide empty cells, so liquidity must be measured as matches per cell with counter-metrics, and those metrics, not engineering preference, set the platform's publication, alert, removal and peak-capacity targets.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a marketplace's health shows in listing counts, traffic and users per listing, and that targets such as indexing latency or peak capacity are engineering choices set by benchmarks and cost.
thesis.so_what: A team that accepts this rejects any latency or freshness objective that does not name the liquidity metric it protects, sizes search for the weekly peak rather than the daily average, and decides where to seed supply cell by cell rather than country by country.
thesis.how_why: Tradeyard Portugal had 2.5 users per live listing against the Netherlands' 2.3, yet 46% of its new listings were contacted within 48 hours against 71%, because only 11% of its cells were liquid against 38%. In dense goods cells the first buyer to message wins, so six minutes to searchable, a sold listing still in alerts and a 48-minute brown-out at the Sunday peak (about 9,800 lost first contacts) each cost matches.

role.contribution: Defines liquidity and its metrics, and makes them the source of the targets that later chapters design for.

transition_in.carries_over: The four models, which differ in where the marketplace's job ends.
transition_in.introduces: What all of them sell underneath, liquidity, and how to measure whether the job is being done well.

posts.title: From Newspaper Columns to Portfolios: How the Classifieds Industry Evolved

thesis.question: How did today's marketplace groups form, what did each phase do to their architectures, and what must a group's shared platforms therefore survive?
thesis.claim: Today's marketplace groups formed in five waves (print columns, online pioneers, portfolio building, consolidation, and take-privates and break-ups), each of which left systems that outlived the strategy that deposited them, so a group's architecture should be read as sediment rather than as a set of mistakes; and because capital strategy changes faster than platforms, as Adevinta's 2023 convergence and 2025 decentralization show, every shared group platform must be built to be separable when a brand is sold.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a group's several search engines and identity systems are technical debt from poor past decisions, to be consolidated onto one target stack for maximum synergy in a portfolio treated as permanent.

Consolidation then built shared platforms for synergy, and take-privates and break-ups turned them into separation costs. Share the generic engine and indexing where it fits, keep relevance local where it differentiates (Veldmark kept Motorvane on its own engine until a 2029 review), and check which value stream search is the bottleneck of.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?

thesis.question: How do we describe a marketplace's capabilities independently of the systems that implement them, and use that description to decide what a group shares?
thesis.claim: A multi-brand group should decide what to share on a three-level map of what its marketplaces do, independent of systems and teams, cross-mapped to the value streams that produce liquidity and scored separately for differentiation, maturity and duplication; duplication alone proves nothing, because a duplicated capability that differentiates a vertical should stay local, and most answers come from splitting a capability at level 3 into shared machinery and local content.

posts.title: Bounded Contexts for Marketplaces: Where One Listing Becomes Many Models

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How should a marketplace be decomposed into domains, and where do the boundaries go?
thesis.claim: A listing marketplace's boundaries belong where the meaning of 'listing' changes (a feed record in supply, an aggregate in the catalog, a case subject in trust, a document in search, an entitlement holder in monetization, a fact row in analytics); the catalog owns the listing's state, every other context builds its own view from a published listing event and never writes listing state back, and each relationship on the context map is recorded as an organizational decision about who adapts to whom.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a marketplace should keep one canonical listing model, in one table or one service, shared by every team, so that all teams see the same listing and data is never duplicated.
thesis.so_what: A late dealer removal becomes one context's freshness contract instead of a bug in six places: a group that accepts this names one owner for every piece of listing data, moves paid-visibility and moderation state out of the shared table, treats the search index as a read model and gives each context exactly one owning team.
thesis.how_why: Teams sharing one model negotiate every change with every other team: Yardstick's ads table has 214 columns read by 38 modules. Trust decisions must survive the listing's deletion, search does not want the seller's phone number, and real estate cares about the property behind three listings, so no single structure holds every meaning with its invariants. posts.title: Same Platform, Different Physics: How Listing Verticals Differ

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.

thesis.question: What genuinely differs between verticals, and what can be shared?
thesis.claim: Verticals differ in physics (who supplies the inventory, whether the item has an identity outside the listing, which external system of record wins a conflict, how long a listing lives, how many attributes it carries, what a lead is worth and where the money moves), so a group should share the machinery beneath (login, events, media, messaging transport, search infrastructure), let each vertical own its content on shared engines, give vertical capabilities such as vehicle identity and property entities one group owner, and move a vertical onto a shared engine only when the engine meets that vertical's requirement profile.

parts.title: Part II — LISTING: Modeling the Thing Being Sold

know: The listing as an aggregate: what it holds and what it only references, its identity scheme, its invariants, and a lifecycle with a publication state and a separate enforcement overlay.

How categories, attributes, media, location and seller accounts are each modeled as governed, versioned reference data: canonical tree and releases; dictionary, binding and value; content-addressed assets and hashes; precise point, public point and place IDs; user, legal entity, billing account and storefront.
Which parts of the listing model carry privacy or legal weight: photo metadata, a private seller's precise location and trader status.
believe: A listing is an offer about a thing, not the thing, and the aggregate should get narrower over the years, not wider.
Taxonomy, attributes, places and media are reference data whose changes are releases with migrations, not admin edits.
Privacy and legal boundaries belong in the data model and on the server, not in what the page shows.
can_do: Decide what lives inside their listing aggregate and write a lifecycle specification and event contract with a removal deadline per consumer.
Plan a category split or a new required attribute as a versioned release with a mapping, an effective date and a migration of every dependent system.
Find where their platform leaks a private seller's location or photo metadata, and model an agency network with franchisees and feed vendors.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
A reader who has read only Part II can turn three proposed listing-table columns into the part's models and say where each belongs.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A product team proposes three new columns on the listings table: `is_ebike`, `seller_lat_lng` copied from the seller's profile, and `agency_parent_id` for franchise branches. Using only Part II, what do you do with each?
acceptance_criteria.expected: None goes on the listing. E-bike is a leaf in the canonical category tree (or an attribute bound by the category schema), shipped as a taxonomy release with a mapping and migration. The coordinate becomes the location value object: a restricted precise point, a public point derived by the precision policy and place IDs, and the precise point never reaches a client. The parent pointer becomes the seller model: each franchisee is its own legal entity and trader, with branches, a network and separate billing accounts; the listing references the seller account and branch by ID.

thesis.question: What is the thing being sold, and how should it be modeled?
thesis.claim: A listing is an offer about a thing, not the thing: a small aggregate with one owner, a publication state with a separate enforcement overlay and a versioned event for every transition, which holds categories, attributes, media, places and seller accounts only as IDs, each with its own owner and rate of change; categories, attributes and places are reference data published in versioned releases and changed under compatibility rules and migrations, while media assets and seller accounts carry their own identity and lifecycle; and the privacy and legal facts several of them carry (photo metadata, a private seller's precise location, trader status) are protected in the data model and on the server, not by what the page shows.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of modeling the listing as one wide record (the `ads` table) with a single status column, category IDs in code, and attributes, photo URLs, coordinates and account flags as columns that each team extends, with taxonomy and attributes edited as content in admin tools and privacy handled by what the listing page displays.
thesis.so_what: An architect who accepts this assigns one owner to each dimension of the listing and to each subdomain, registers every copy as an event consumer with a removal deadline, ships taxonomy and attribute changes as releases with mappings and effective dates, and scans public payloads for precise points and photo metadata. Veldmark does this in 2027: lead time for a new category falls from six weeks to two days, and Hearthly plans to cut its media run cost from €6.2 million to €3.6 million by the end of 2028.
thesis.how_why: Search, alerts, trust, monetization, analytics, SEO and partner feeds all copy the listing, so every vague state or field is reinterpreted per copy: Femke's sold bike still reached 214 alert digests, and about 41,000 ended Tradeyard NL listings sat in some copy a day later. Categories, attributes, media, places and accounts change at different rates for different owners, so binding them into the listing turns each change into a cross-team release and lets keys pile up: 3,900 attribute keys, 41% of them on fewer than 0.1% of listings. And a postcode centroid in an API payload, GPS coordinates in a photo or a franchisee shown under its parent's name are defects that no interface can hide.

supporting_claims.claim: A listing is a seller's time-bounded offer, kept separate from the underlying entity, placements and moderation cases: one service owns the aggregate and holds category, attributes, media, place and seller account only as IDs owned elsewhere, seller and platform changes share a publication state while enforcement is a separate overlay, and every transition is a versioned event with a removal deadline per consumer.

The category is a schema key, not a label, so the taxonomy is one canonical classification tree with stable IDs and leaf-only listing, from which navigation, country views and external mappings are derived, and every change ships as a versioned release with a mapping and a migration plan.

An attribute's meaning, its binding to a category and its value are three layers with different owners; one dictionary compiled into forms, validators, search and feed mappings, and changed under compatibility rules, keeps the Attribute Junkyard from forming or regrowing, whatever each brand stores it in.

Media has its own identity and lifecycle: listings reference content-addressed asset IDs, every upload is stripped of location and device metadata before anything is stored or served, derivatives are generated on demand, retention follows listing state, and a perceptual-hash match to an unrelated seller is a trust decision that can hold a listing before buyers can contact it.

Location is three representations (a restricted precise point, a public point derived by a precision policy and place IDs from a gazetteer released in versions and backfilled like the category tree); everything a buyer or partner can read is computed from the public point on the server, and the licence terms of every coordinate are recorded.

Who acts, who is responsible, who pays and who is shown are separate entities: accounts have their own lifecycle, trader status is a governed attribute with evidence, organizations own listings, integrations are principals with scoped grants, and a group shares login and verified legal-entity facts, not accounts.

role.contribution: Designs the first stage of the machine, the listing model that every later stage reads as a contract.

flow.rationale: Each chapter designs a subdomain that the chapter before has made a slot for or a dependency on. The aggregate comes first because it decides what is inside the listing and what is only a reference; before it, the five subdomains would have nothing to be referenced by. Categories follow because the category selects the contract for the rest: the attribute schema, fees, moderation and facets. Attributes need the category tree, since a schema is bound to a category; placed before categories, the binding layer would bind to nothing. Media comes after attributes because it applies the attribute chapter's move, one contract compiled for every consumer, to the largest body of listing data (asset IDs, one derivative scheme, a `MediaReady` event); placed before attributes, the media contract would read as a storage design rather than a second instance of the same discipline, and the contrast that opens it (words and numbers, then pictures) would be lost. Media must also precede location because it strips the GPS coordinates that location's privacy rule would otherwise leave exposed; placed after location, the precision policy would be read as complete while the photos still leak the door. Location comes after media and after categories for the same reasons: it relies on EXIF stripping and governs its gazetteer like the category tree. Sellers come last because an agency's display level and a franchisee's trader record are account facts the earlier chapters only point to, and because the account model's integration principals are what Part III's ingestion authenticates. Placed straight after the aggregate, where ownership is decided, the chapter would have to model agencies' location precision and per-branch media and attribute duties before the reader had seen location, media or attributes, and the part would end on location, which hands nothing to supply.

hook.content: Most marketplaces modeled the listing once, at launch, and have extended it ever since: fifteen years later the `ads` table has two hundred columns, category IDs live in the code, and nobody can say which copy of a listing is the true one.

opening.bridge: From Part I's domain boundaries and its decision about who owns the listing's truth to the design of the thing being sold inside them.
opening.roadmap: Six chapters in order: the listing aggregate and its lifecycle, then the five subdomains it references by ID: categories, attributes, media, location and the sellers and organizations who list.

closing.synthesis: With the seller account modeled, every reference the listing holds has an owner, a version and a contract: the aggregate and its events, the canonical tree and its releases, the attribute dictionary, the media asset model, the location value object and the supply-side account model.
closing.so_what: Veldmark's 2027 decisions (Veldmark Place in May, Listing event contract v1 on 1 July, the business party registry in August, the taxonomy and attribute service in October, the group media decision in November) give every later stage a contract to read instead of a table to copy.
closing.callback: The part opening's test: be able to say who owns each part of a listing, how it is versioned and which systems copy it.

takeaway.content: For each part of your listing, name its owner, its version and the systems that copy it; Part III then puts the model under load through forms, APIs and feeds, starting with the integration principals this chapter defined.

transition_in.carries_over: Part I's bounded contexts, which decided that one context owns the listing's truth, and its vertical requirement profiles, which showed items with identities and systems of record outside the listing.
transition_in.introduces: The supply-side core those contexts depend on: the listing aggregate and the governed reference data around it.

The six chapters in reading order and the question each answers, and the Veldmark decisions that give the listing model its contracts in 2027.

posts.title: The Listing Aggregate: Identity, Lifecycle and Invariants
posts.question: What is a listing, what must always be true about it, and how does it change over time?

know: The difference between a listing, the underlying entity, a product, a placement and a moderation case, and what lives inside the aggregate.
The identity scheme (internal ID, public ID, external key, entity reference), the publication lifecycle with its enforcement overlay, and the three ways to store history.
believe: Ghost inventory is an event-consumption problem, not a search problem, and removal deadlines matter more than insertion ones.
can_do: Write a lifecycle specification and a versioned event contract for their own marketplace, with a removal deadline per consumer and a re-check at send for pre-assembled outputs.
Separate invariants enforced in the aggregate from policies enforced asynchronously.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a sold listing that still reached a downstream output, the reader locates the failure and names the fix in the chapter's terms.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A seller marks a bike sold at 18:10; it leaves search at 18:11, but a 07:00 alert digest the next morning still includes it. Using only this chapter: where did the model fail, and what fixes it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Not search: the digest was assembled from a snapshot before the sale and nothing re-checked it. Every copy must be a registered consumer of versioned lifecycle events (sold, expired, withdrawn, blocked) with a declared removal deadline, and pre-assembled outputs re-check state just before sending; the sale price is recorded as an outcome, not a price change.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Veldmark's four systems giving four answers about one sold bike; what a listing is and is not; identity and keys; the two-dimensional lifecycle with renewals and outcomes; invariants; versions and price history; availability and units; one owner and many copies; public evidence and the bike replayed transition by transition; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes and the Chief Architect's view. Evidence: documented public APIs and standards and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: What is a listing, what must always be true about it, and how does it change over time?
thesis.claim: A listing is a seller's time-bounded offer about a thing, not the thing: one listing service owns a small aggregate that references the underlying entity, category, attributes, media, place, account and paid placements by ID, enforces synchronously the rules one listing can check alone (exactly one owning account, a leaf category valid in the taxonomy version it records, required attributes present at submission, a `created_at` that never moves, no seller command that lifts an enforcement block), and records seller and platform changes in one publication state with enforcement as a separate overlay owned by trust and safety; every transition is a versioned event, and each consumer has a declared removal deadline, so ghost inventory is a failure of event consumption, not of search.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of one wide listings table with a single status field and paid flags as columns, in which the search index is the de facto record of what is for sale and a sold listing is handled by deleting it from search.
thesis.so_what: An architect who accepts this writes one lifecycle specification and versioned event contract for every brand (Veldmark's Listing event contract v1, live on 1 July 2027), registers every copy as a consumer with a removal deadline (under 10 seconds for search, 2 minutes for alerts and recommendations, 15 minutes for partner feeds), makes pre-assembled outputs such as digests re-check state before sending, and measures lingering copies weekly.
thesis.how_why: Every context copies the listing, so a vague state is reinterpreted per copy: Femke's €240 bike, marked sold at 18:10 and out of search at 18:11, still reached 214 digests the next morning from a snapshot taken before the sale, and analytics recorded it as expired; Veldmark's audit found about 41,000 ended Tradeyard NL listings in some copy 24 hours later. Seller intent, platform time and enforcement change for different reasons and owners, so one status field lets a listing be both sold and promoted, or lets a seller's edit undo a block.

role.contribution: Defines the aggregate, its references, lifecycle and events, the slots that every other Part II chapter fills.

transition_in.carries_over: The part opening's claim that a listing is an offer about a thing, a small aggregate that references governed subdomains.
transition_in.introduces: What is inside the aggregate and what is only referenced, its identity, invariants and two-dimensional lifecycle, and the events that leave it.

posts.title: Category Trees That Can Change: Designing Marketplace Taxonomies
posts.question: How do you design a category taxonomy that serves sellers, buyers, search, ads and analytics, and evolve it without breaking everything?

know: What a category controls, the structural choices (strict tree, polyhierarchy, facets; classification versus navigation; one tree or many) and mappings to external taxonomies.
What a taxonomy release contains and how splits, merges, moves and retirements are run as migrations.
believe: A category is a schema key, not a label, so a taxonomy change is a schema migration.
can_do: Diagnose the Category Straitjacket in their own platform.
Plan a category split covering listings, saved searches, URLs, partner codes, models and analytics.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a requested category split, the reader lists what the release must carry and what must be migrated besides the tree.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Product wants the generic 'Bikes' leaf split into city, e-bikes, cargo and kids' bikes next month in four countries. Using only this chapter: what does the release contain, and what else has to move?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A new canonical tree version with stable IDs, a mapping from every retired node, the attribute diff and effective dates. Existing listings are reclassified by rules, a model above a confidence threshold and seller confirmation, gated by an audit; saved searches are rewritten to preserve results, retired URLs redirected, partner codes accepted for a window with warnings, search mappings and models updated, and analytics given a mapping view instead of rewritten history. Country views keep local labels and navigation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Veldmark's six weeks for a new leaf; what a category controls; four structural choices; the taxonomy as versioned reference data and its service; mapping to external taxonomies; migrations and the runbook; category prediction; the bikes split in practice and the harmonization of four trees; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes and the Chief Architect's view. Evidence: public company engineering sources, external taxonomy standards and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How do you design a category taxonomy that serves sellers, buyers, search, ads and analytics, and evolve it without breaking everything?
thesis.claim: The category is a schema key, not a label: it selects the attributes, validation, fees, moderation, facets, ranking and ad targeting of every listing in it, so a marketplace needs one canonical classification tree with stable IDs and leaf-only listing, with navigation trees, country views, labels, slugs and external mappings derived from it, published by an owned taxonomy service as versioned releases that carry a mapping from every retired node, an attribute diff and effective dates; splits and merges are then run as migrations of listings, saved searches, URLs, partner codes, models and analytics.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that categories are editorial content edited in an admin tool, that each country keeps its own tree, and that a split is a reorganization product managers decide and engineering ships in a coordinated release.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this removes category IDs from code, runs the taxonomy as a product with an owner, classifies changes by blast radius (cosmetic the same day, additive in two days, structural in two to four weeks) and tracks lead time for a new category: Veldmark's fell from six weeks to two days, and its bikes split reclassified 410,000 listings behind a 95% audit gate and rewrote about 1.3 million saved searches.
thesis.how_why: Category IDs end up in fee rules, moderation rules, search mappings, SEO tables, dashboards and partner feeds, so an edit made like content ripples like a schema change, and the tree hardens into the Category Straitjacket while the 'Other' leaf grows. Separating classification from navigation lets Poland keep bikes under its 'Sport i hobby' browse node while models and ad segments address one e-bike leaf in four countries.

role.contribution: Turns the category ID the aggregate holds into a governed, versioned tree and a migration practice, and gives the attribute chapter the key its schemas bind to.

transition_in.carries_over: The category ID and taxonomy version that the aggregate records and takes as given.
transition_in.introduces: The problem that the tree behind them must change while millions of listings sit in it, and the design that lets it: a canonical tree released as versioned data with migrations.

posts.title: Attributes Without Chaos: Schemas, Dictionaries and Validation
posts.question: How should listing attributes be modeled so they can be validated, searched, faceted and evolved per category and vertical?

know: The three layers of definition (dictionary), binding (category schema) and value (with provenance), and the storage options with their trade-offs.
How a schema service compiles one definition into forms, validators, search mappings, facets and feed mappings, and the compatibility rules for changing attributes.
believe: The Attribute Junkyard forms when systems interpret attributes on their own, and a shared dictionary does not require a shared storage model.
can_do: Plan the cleanup of their own attribute keys and the governance that keeps them from regrowing.
Ship a new required attribute without breaking producers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a request to change an existing attribute, the reader classifies the change and says how to ship it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A steward wants battery capacity to become required on e-bikes now, and separately to change mileage from kilometres to miles in one country. Using only this chapter: how is each shipped?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Making an attribute required breaks producers, so it ships first as recommended with a published effective date and is enforced on create and revise once the feed readiness report allows; existing listings are not invalidated. Changing a unit changes meaning, so it is a new attribute, never an edit of the old one, with values normalized and both bound during migration.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Veldmark's eleven keys for frame size; the three layers; the dictionary entry; category schemas and how they evolve; reference data; normalization of units and values; attributes for search, trust, ads and feeds; storage models; a schema service that compiles, with mappings to partner feed standards; public examples and Veldmark's cleanup in steps; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes and the Chief Architect's view. Evidence: public company sources, feed and regulatory standards and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How should listing attributes be modeled so they can be validated, searched, faceted and evolved per category and vertical?
thesis.claim: Listing attributes need three layers with different owners: a dictionary that fixes each attribute's meaning, type, unit and allowed values; versioned category schemas that bind attributes as required, recommended or optional; and listing values with provenance. One schema service compiles these into forms, validators, search mappings, facets and feed mappings, and changes follow event-schema compatibility rules: an optional addition is safe, a new requirement ships with an effective date, and a change of meaning, type or unit creates a new attribute. The storage model may differ per brand.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that attributes are a storage choice (wide columns, EAV or a JSON document) that each team, country or feed extends as needed, with forms, feeds and search each validating and interpreting values themselves, and that a group-wide definition is only worth having if it comes with one shared storage model.
thesis.so_what: A group that accepts this shares the dictionary, compiler, validator library and reference-data service but not storage, gives each vertical a named steward, makes a reviewed new attribute live in two working days, and tracks coverage, validity and the long-tail ratio. Veldmark mapped 2,310 of Tradeyard's 3,900 keys to 1,240 canonical attributes, retired 990 and kept 600 as country extensions, migrating first the 31 retired keys something still read.
thesis.how_why: Attributes are read by more systems than any other part of the listing, so a key without a governed definition gets a different meaning in each: Tradeyard stored frame size under eleven keys, and 41% of its 3,900 keys were used on fewer than 0.1% of listings. Making a field required breaks every producer that does not yet send it, so battery capacity for e-bikes shipped as recommended with a required date of 1 March 2028 to give dealer feeds time.

role.contribution: Defines the attribute contract that ingestion validates, enrichment normalizes toward and search turns into filters and facets.

transition_in.carries_over: The category, which decides which schema applies but does not define it, and the new e-bike attributes the bikes split introduced.
transition_in.introduces: The next layer down: the attribute dictionary, the category schemas that bind it and the governance that keeps one definition true in every system.

posts.title: Photos Sell: Media Pipelines for Listings
posts.question: How do you ingest, process, store, moderate and serve billions of listing images and other media?

know: The asset model (content-derived identity, sanitized master, moderation state, retention class), the upload-to-edge pipeline and what blocks publication.
Where media costs come from (copies, stored renditions, never-deleted originals) and how exact and perceptual hashes differ in use.
believe: Hashes are trust infrastructure, and a match that cannot hold a listing or carries no seller context lets fraud run.
can_do: Explain a media bill and plan the changes that cut it: content addressing, on-demand derivatives, lifecycle by listing state.
Decide which media checks must complete before a listing is contactable.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a duplicate-photo detector that fired but did not stop a fraud, the reader names what was missing.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A rental portal's hash index matched stolen photos within minutes of upload, yet the fake listings went live and buyers paid deposits. Using only this chapter: what was missing, and what should the pipeline do?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The match only created a queue item while the listing went live, and it returned a distance with no relationship between the two sellers. For high-risk categories, a perceptual-hash match to an unrelated seller or a block-listed hash should hold the listing for a trust decision within the publication budget, each match carrying the seller relationship, with the index shared across brands.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Hearthly's 1.8 billion images and the Barcelona fake-rental ring; assets, masters, derivatives and hashes; the upload-to-edge pipeline and what blocks publication; privacy in photos; derivatives, formats and the CDN; storage tiers and lifecycle; perceptual hashing; understanding images; video, tours and floor plans; public examples and Hearthly's plan in numbers; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes and the Chief Architect's view. Evidence: public engineering sources, standards and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How do you ingest, process, store, moderate and serve billions of listing images and other media?
thesis.claim: Media is a subdomain with its own identity and lifecycle, not a storage-and-CDN concern: a listing references content-addressed asset IDs; every upload path converges on one step that sanitizes files, strips location metadata and hashes them; derivatives are generated on demand at the edge rather than stored; sanitized masters move to colder tiers and are deleted by retention class as listings end; and a perceptual-hash match to an unrelated seller is a trust decision, shared across brands, that can hold a listing before buyers can contact it.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that media is a storage and CDN concern: keep every upload and every rendition indefinitely because storage is cheap, and treat duplicate and stolen-photo detection as a moderation-queue add-on that runs after publication.
thesis.so_what: A group that accepts this shares the media contract (asset model, media API, derivative URL scheme, `MediaReady` event) first and the infrastructure later, sets retention classes with the data protection and trust-and-safety owners, and watches stored bytes per live listing and the share of unrelated-seller matches decided before a listing is contactable; Hearthly plans to cut its media run cost from €6.2 million to €3.6 million by the end of 2028.
thesis.how_why: Hearthly stores 1.8 billion images: about 38% of originals are byte-for-byte copies created by feeds that re-send every photo URL, nine JPEG renditions are kept per image, and about 96% belong to listings no longer live, so storage grew 19% in 2026 while live listings grew 4%. In July 2027 its hash index matched the Barcelona ring's stolen photos within minutes, but the match only queued a 'possible duplicate' with no seller context while the listings went live, and 63 people lost about €71,000.

role.contribution: Designs the largest referenced subdomain as one pipeline with one contract, and supplies the photo-metadata stripping that the location chapter's privacy rule depends on.

transition_in.carries_over: The attribute dictionary, which describes what a listing says in words and numbers.
transition_in.introduces: Pictures, which buyers judge first: a second and far larger body of listing data with its own pipeline, storage economics, privacy risks and fraud signals.

posts.title: Where Is It? Location, Geocoding and Privacy
posts.question: How do you model and process location so search, maps, trust and analytics work across countries?

know: Country-shaped addresses, geocoding outputs, gazetteers and place hierarchies, precision levels and geo indexes.
The three representations per listing (restricted precise point, public point, place IDs) and the semantics of radius, polygon and place searches.
believe: Location is a small subsystem, not a field, and geocoding is a licensing decision before it is a technical one.
can_do: Find where their platform leaks a private seller's location, including through distances and API payloads.
Check whether their stored coordinates are licensed for storage, and why their filters, maps and landing pages disagree.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a location leak that the listing page did not show, the reader explains how it happened and what the model changes.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A marketplace shows only a postcode district on private sellers' listings, yet a buyer turned up at a seller's door. Using only this chapter: how could that happen, and what does the location model change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The precise point (a postcode centroid) was returned in an API payload and used for distances shown to one decimal, so a payload read or three searches located the door. Store a restricted precise point, derive a public point deterministically by precision policy, and compute every shown distance, map pin, feed and payload from the public point only, enforced on the server and checked by a weekly exposure scan with a target of zero.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Veldmark's five answers to 'where is it?'; what location means: kinds, addresses, geocoding, gazetteers, precision, geo indexes; three representations and their services, the public point and the rule for distances; radius, polygon and place semantics; geocoding providers and licences; the Rotterdam bike, the Lyon apartment, the Barcelona ring and quality metrics; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes and the Chief Architect's view. Evidence: provider terms, standards and documentation, and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How do you model and process location so search, maps, trust and analytics work across countries?
thesis.claim: A listing's location is a small subsystem, not a field: it stores a restricted precise point, a public point derived from it deterministically by a group precision policy, and stable place IDs from a versioned gazetteer, so radius search, landing pages, duplicate detection, fraud signals and analytics each read the representation meant for them; distances, map pins, payloads, feeds and structured data are computed from the public point only, enforced on the server; and geocoder licence terms are recorded with every coordinate, because storage rights depend on provider, country and use.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that location is one coordinate field, geocoded once and read by every consumer, with privacy handled by what the listing page displays and geocoder choice a matter of price and accuracy.
thesis.so_what: A group that accepts this runs one gazetteer and geocoding gateway (Veldmark Place, approved in May 2027), makes the precision policy group policy with brand parameters, chooses providers per country and use behind the gateway and reviews their licences in every acquisition, and publishes location quality weekly, with a precise-point exposure target of zero and any exposure treated as a privacy incident.
thesis.how_why: Tradeyard showed '3014 Rotterdam' on the page but returned the seller's postcode centroid to six decimals in its search API and showed distances to one decimal, so a stranger found a seller's door; Hearthly Spain showed exact pins for private landlords. Search radius, landing pages, duplicate detection and fraud each need a different representation: the Barcelona ring's 35%-below-market signal exists only because rent medians are computed per small H3 cell.

role.contribution: Models location as three representations under a precision policy and a governed gazetteer, which search, maps, alerts, duplicate detection and fraud later read.

transition_in.carries_over: The media pipeline's stripping of GPS coordinates from photos, one way a listing can reveal where a seller lives.
transition_in.introduces: The listing's own location, where the same privacy risk sits beside search, maps and licensing: a subsystem of addresses, geocoders, places and a precision policy.

posts.title: Private Sellers, Dealers and Agencies: Modeling Who Lists
posts.question: How should a marketplace model the people and organizations that supply listings?

know: Private and professional sellers, trader status, organizations, branches and networks, users and memberships, and integration principals.
The three options for who-lists data in a multi-brand group (separate, shared identity and registry, one group account) and when each fits.
believe: The account model is where marketplaces most often confuse identity with commerce, and trader status is a governed attribute, not a checkbox.
can_do: Model an agency network with franchisees, departing staff and a feed vendor so that trader information, reviews, leads and invoices land on the right entity.
Decide what a group shares across brand accounts and the purpose limits on it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an agency network's complaints, the reader traces them to one modeling error and assigns each to the right entity.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An agency network with nine owned branches and five franchisees complains: franchise listings show the parent as trader, one franchisee's reviews appear on every branch, a departed agent still receives leads for 212 listings, and franchise subscriptions are invoiced to the parent. Using only this chapter: what is the single cause, and where does each fact belong?
acceptance_criteria.expected: One entity was login, legal identity, billing party, public profile and listing owner. Each franchisee is its own legal entity and trader; reviews attach to the branch or storefront; listings belong to the organization and are assigned to branches, not to a user, so leads route through the branch; each franchisee has its own contract and billing account. The feed vendor is an integration principal with scoped grants.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Fourteen branches and three wrong answers at Hearthly; the vocabulary of supply: private and professional sellers, trader status, organizations, branches and networks, seller accounts and contracts, users and roles, integration principals; the seller account model with one entity per question, its lifecycle, lead routing and reputation; trade-offs and vertical differences; documented patterns and three Veldmark accounts; group-wide identity versus per-brand accounts; failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions to ask. Evidence: EU consumer, platform and tax law, public company sources and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How should a marketplace model the people and organizations that supply listings?
thesis.claim: A seller account model must answer four questions with separate entities: who acts (users with memberships and roles), who is responsible (the legal entity, which is the trader), who pays (contracts and billing accounts) and who is shown (storefronts and branches). Trader status is a governed attribute with declaration, evidence, verification and history; organizations, not staff, own listings; integrations are principals with grants per account and branch; and a group shares login and verified legal-entity facts in a registry while keeping brand accounts separate.
thesis.disputed_by: The common model of one user or advertiser record that is at once login, legal identity, billing party, public profile and listing owner, extended with a pro flag, parent pointers for branches and shared credentials for feed vendors; and, at group level, the alternative of one group account across all brands.
thesis.so_what: A group that accepts this standardizes the supply-side model and its events before entitlements and messaging copy their own, launches a business party registry with purpose limits and logged cross-brand queries (approved at Veldmark in August 2027), moves feed partners from shared passwords to scoped grants, and tracks the share of professional listings with a verified trader record (target 100%) and orphaned listings.
thesis.how_why: Hearthly's single advertiser entity put the parent company on five franchisees' trader panels, showed one franchisee's reviews on every branch, left 212 listings and their leads with an agent who had left, and invoiced franchise subscriptions to a parent that refused to pay them. Trader status decides which consumer law applies, what the Digital Services Act requires the platform to verify and what is reported to tax authorities, so a checkbox cannot carry it.

role.contribution: Models the last referenced subdomain, who lists, and performs the part's closing: the listing's references are complete and hand supply its first dependency.

transition_in.carries_over: The location chapter's precision choice that each agency makes in its account settings, and the four subdomains already modeled.
transition_in.introduces: The last subdomain the listing references: the people and organizations that supply it, from a private seller to an agency network with franchisees.

parts.title: Part III — SUPPLY: Getting Inventory In

know: The four ingestion channels (insertion flow, partner API, bulk feed, replication from an external system of record), full-snapshot versus delta semantics, and the clauses of a feed contract beyond its schema.
The difference between normalization and enrichment, the seven provenance source classes, and why re-processing and human review, not model calls, drive the cost of enrichment.
The five kinds of duplicate, the real-world entity per vertical, the matching pipeline from blocking to an entity registry, and the representative-listing rule.
The publication pipeline's decision path and propagation path, the three parts of a freshness SLA, and the mechanisms of unpublish propagation.
What professional sellers check the marketplace against, the pro workspace over domain systems of record, and the four neutrality controls for software the group sells to professionals.
believe: Supply is one chain, not five features: a weakness at any link (an unstated contract, an unrecorded source, an unregistered copy) surfaces downstream as a search, trust or billing problem.
Partner state and platform state will drift, so reconciliation, provenance and propagation evidence are built in, not added after incidents.
Removing a listing everywhere matters more than publishing it quickly, and professionals renew only when the marketplace's numbers reconcile with their own systems.

parts.title: Part IV — DISCOVERY: Matching Intent to Inventory

know: The search index as a rebuildable read model: the listing search document, index topology, the write path with its update storms and removal lane, facets on their own path, alias reindexing and the search contract in front of the engine.

Query understanding as compilation into categories and attribute filters: one vocabulary with aliases per language, a confidence-to-action policy with removable chips, null-result recovery, and dense retrieval and LLM query compilers as layers over that core.
Ranking as a relevance model plus a versioned ranking policy, with a relevance floor and a cap on paid positions, delivery events and the ranking-parameters description EU law requires.

Recommendations under churn as candidate generation, one serving-time filter on the status read model and a re-ranker with exposure policy; map search as a geo query compiler over a few place primitives; and saved searches as normalized stored queries matched by percolation.
believe: Discovery is one pipeline with six surfaces, not six products: every surface reads the same listing stream and must forget a sold listing faster than it learns a new one.
Compiling words, places and saved searches into the marketplace's own structure gains more than clever retrieval, and embeddings and language models belong on top of that structure.
The order of results is a policy with owners, judged on contacts, not on clicks, sends or revenue per search.
can_do: Set an insertion and a removal objective for every discovery surface and prove the search index can be rebuilt from the event stream.
