Write a ranking policy that bounds paid visibility and a measurement plan that judges every discovery change on contacts and seller-side guardrails.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
A reader who has read only Part IV can assign six discovery incidents to the surface that owns each and name the control that surface applies.
acceptance_criteria.probe: In one month at a general-classifieds marketplace: a full reindex run on a Sunday evening pushes search p99 to seconds; 'e-bike' returns tens of thousands of ordinary bikes while 'ebike' returns two thousand; paid listings hold 38% of first-page positions and nobody can say why a listing is third; a 'similar items' carousel keeps showing a car sold yesterday while new cars never appear in it; drawn-area searches with raw finger traces take almost two seconds; and a bike sold on Monday appears in Tuesday's alert digest. Using only Part IV, which chapter's design owns each, and what does it do?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Search architecture: reindex into a new index behind an alias, away from the peak, so commits do not clear the caches browse traffic needs; the index is a read model rebuilt from the event stream. Query understanding: one vocabulary entry with aliases per language maps the variants to the e-bikes category, analyzers are checked for token parity, and interpretations are applied by confidence as removable chips. Ranking: a relevance model without entitlement features plus a versioned ranking policy with a relevance floor and a cap on paid positions, reason codes and delivery events, judged on contacts. Recommendations: content features and candidate indices updated by listing events give new cars a place, and one serving-time filter on the shared status read model removes sold cars. Map search: a geo query compiler simplifies the polygon before the engine sees it and aligns viewports to cached tiles. Saved searches and alerts: the digest re-checks availability at send time, and removal retracts the listing from pending notifications.

thesis.question: How should buyers' intent be matched to inventory that changes by the minute, and who should decide the order in which they see it?
thesis.claim: Discovery is one pipeline with six surfaces, not six products: the search index, query understanding, the ranked results page, recommendation carousels, the map and alerts all read the same listing event stream and the same status read model, and every index among them (search, recommendation candidates, alert percolators) is a read model that the group's search platform team proves it can rebuild and that forgets a sold listing faster than it learns a new one (10 seconds p95 for removal from search at Veldmark, with a re-check against the status read model at serving and send time on every other surface); buyers' words, places and saved searches are compiled with stated confidence into the marketplace's own categories, attributes and place primitives, with embeddings and language models layered over that structured core; and the order of results is a versioned policy, separate from the relevance model and owned by named people, that caps paid visibility under a relevance floor and is judged on contacts rather than clicks or sends.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of building search, recommendations, maps and alerts as separate products on separate copies of the data, each tuned against its own metric (click-through, alerts sent, revenue per search), with relevance treated as a text-matching problem that better models will solve and with paid visibility expressed as boosts in the engine's configuration.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this shares the machinery of discovery (engine operations and the search contract, one query vocabulary, the ranking service and its log, the status read model, the geo query compiler, the saved-search service) while each marketplace keeps its schemas, analyzers, models, policy values and user experience; sets a removal objective for every surface; and judges every discovery change on contacts, new-listing exposure and the paid share of first-page positions.
thesis.how_why: Every surface fails in the same few ways when it is built as its own product. Tradeyard NL's search browned out for 48 minutes on 17 January 2027 because a reindex wrote into the live collection; eleven ways of writing e-bike produced four result sets until one vocabulary entry sent ten of them to the new category; five boost layers each tested on revenue raised the paid share of first-page positions from 12% to 38% while sessions with a contact fell; a nightly co-view carousel left 41% of new Motorvane listings without an impression and kept the sold Golf on show; raw polygons gave Hearthly a 1.8-second p99; and 214 digests advertised Femke's sold bike. Each repair compiled input into shared structure, re-read the shared status, or moved the order into an owned policy.

supporting_claims.claim: The search index, the first of the discovery read models, is built like all of them from the one listing event stream, and every later surface re-checks the same status read model: documents are built only from the listing event stream and the system of record under a listing-owned version, a regular drill proves the rebuild, removal latency is its own objective, tighter than insertion's (10 seconds against 15 seconds p95 at Veldmark), with a priority lane, volatile fields stay off the document and facets run on their own path, and product applications call a platform-owned search contract, so the engine behind it is a replaceable adapter.

Understanding a listing query mostly means compiling it into the marketplace's own categories and attribute filters from one versioned vocabulary, applying each interpretation by its confidence as a removable filter, boost or suggestion, recovering from thin results in a defined order, and adding dense retrieval and LLM query compilers only as layers that emit the same validated form.

The order of results is a versioned ranking policy separate from a relevance model that never sees entitlements: the policy bounds paid visibility with a relevance floor and a cap on paid positions, emits delivery events and reason codes, and is judged on contacts and seller-side guardrails, with its main parameters described in plain language as EU law requires; a ranking council per brand (the discovery product owner as chair, with search, monetization, trust and data science) owns the metric, guardrails and policy file, and changes that affect more than one brand go through a decision record.

Recommending short-lived inventory depends on plumbing more than on algorithms: content and image features give a listing a place before behavior exists, candidate indices take inserts and deletes from listing events, one serving-time filter on the shared status read model removes unavailable listings, and a re-ranker with an exposure policy is judged on contacts and inventory coverage, with a non-personalized mode that stands on its own.

Where place is the main filter, one geo query compiler turns named areas, drawn shapes, commutes and viewports into a few cacheable primitives; pins and clusters are computed from the public point and counted per canonical property; and map traffic is budgeted, ranked and evaluated as its own product, with routing cost decided by a volume forecast.

A saved search is a normalized stored query in a system of record from which percolators are rebuilt; alerts fire when a listing enters a match set, pass a risk gate, re-check availability at send time and survive taxonomy changes through migration that preserves recall; and they are judged on latency, alert-to-contact and ghost-alert rates, not on sends.

additional_patterns.applies_to: search-architecture to ranking: the index and contract, then what the buyer's words become against it, then the order of what it returns

flow.rationale: Each chapter reuses what the one before it established. Search architecture comes first because every other surface queries its index, document and contract: query understanding sits between that contract and the engine inside a 25 ms budget, and map search and alerts query the same index by area and in reverse; placed later, those chapters would compile queries against, and percolate over, an index and contract the reader has not met. Query understanding precedes ranking because ranking orders the candidates retrieval returns, and the retrieved set depends on the filters and interpretations compiled from the query; placed after ranking, the reader would meet a relevance model trained on results before learning which listings a query can reach. Ranking precedes recommendations because a recommendation module is a ranked list without a query: candidate generation, re-ranking, exposure policy and position-corrected logging are defined in ranking and only reused there; reversed, recommendations would introduce that machinery without the query that anchors it. Map search follows recommendations because it reuses that chapter's lesson that a surface without a ranked list of typed results needs its own ranking and evaluation (the principles 'content first, availability always, measured on matches' return there), and it applies query understanding's compile-to-structure pattern to place; placed before query understanding, the geo query compiler would look like a special case rather than the same design. Saved searches and alerts come last because they consume every earlier surface: the normalized query format shared with the search API and the geo query compiler, percolators on the shared search platform, saved polygons and isochrone parameters from map search, and engagement signals that ranking and recommendations use. Placed before map search, alerts would store polygons and isochrone parameters the reader has not seen normalized, and the part would end in the middle of the pipeline. Ending there also places the risk gate, where alerts amplify whatever they carry, immediately before Part V's trust platform.

hook.content: Listing discovery looks like web search but behaves like a high-write operational system: documents live for days, most queries contain no text, and it is judged by how fast a new listing appears and a sold one disappears.

opening.bridge: From Part III's supply, clean, deduplicated and searchable within a freshness target, to the other side of the market: the buyer who types three words, draws a shape on a map or saves a search and waits.
opening.roadmap: Six chapters, each a surface over the same listing stream: the search index and its contract, query understanding, two-sided ranking, recommendations for short-lived inventory, map and commute search, and saved searches with alerts; each answers three questions: is this listing still available, who decided its position, and did it lead to a contact.

closing.synthesis: Alerts use every surface before them: the normalized query of the search contract and the geo query compiler, percolators on the shared search platform, the status read model that recommendations re-read, and contact-based measurement that ranking introduced. Together the six chapters make discovery one pipeline in which every surface forgets a sold listing quickly, names who decided the order and is judged by the contacts it produces.
closing.so_what: Discovery now puts a new listing in front of its most motivated buyers within minutes, which is worth as much to a fraudster as to an honest seller; the speed Part IV builds is safe only behind a risk gate and decisions every surface obeys.
closing.callback: The part opening's three questions (is this listing still available, who decided its position, did it lead to a contact) and its promise that the reader can say, for each surface, how fast it forgets a sold listing and who owns the order it shows.

takeaway.content: Alerts amplify whatever they carry, as the 180 fake Eixample rentals and their 41,000 alerts showed; Part V begins with trust-and-safety-architecture, which builds the trust platform whose decisions publication, search and alerts must obey.

role.contribution: Turns the supply delivered by Part III into matches on the buyer's side, and makes the ordering of results an owned decision.

transition_in.carries_over: Part III's published, deduplicated and removable listings, its 90-second freshness budget with removal from search in 10 seconds, and professional-seller-tooling's closing claim that discovery inherits whatever ghost, duplicate or disputed count supply leaves behind.
transition_in.introduces: The buyer's side: search, query understanding, ranking, recommendations, map search and alerts as surfaces that read that supply and turn it into contacts.

posts.title: Search Architecture for Listings: Indices, Freshness and Scale
posts.question: How do you build search for millions of short-lived listings with rich filters?

know: Why listing search behaves like a high-write operational store: short-lived documents, mostly text-free browse queries, and writes dominated by price, status, bump and counter changes.

The listing search document and its promotion rule for typed versus flattened attributes, the three questions that decide index topology, the write path (external versioning, update-storm lanes, separate removal latency), the read path (facets on their own path, caching, latency budgets), alias reindexing and capacity planning for evening peaks.

A stable search contract in front of the engine matters more than the choice of engine.

Reindex into a new index behind an alias, replay the stream, swap, and keep maintenance away from the peak planned with marketing. Before any engine change, put product applications behind a platform-owned search contract, build documents only from the event stream and system of record with a listing-owned version, prove the rebuild with a regular drill and set removal latency as its own objective; then the engine is an adapter decision judged by workload fit.

thesis.question: How do you build search for millions of short-lived listings with rich filters?
thesis.claim: Listing search should be built as a read model that can be thrown away: every document comes from the listing event stream and the system of record under a listing-owned version, a quarterly drill proves the index can be rebuilt, only attributes the schema marks as filter, facet or sort keys become typed fields, removals take a priority lane with their own objective (10 seconds p95 at Veldmark against 15 seconds for insertion), counters stay off the document, facets run on their own path, reindexing goes through aliases away from the peak, and product applications call a platform-owned search contract, so the engine behind it becomes a replaceable adapter.
thesis.disputed_by: The common view that engine choice is the main search decision, settled by benchmarks, and that the index may hold whatever fields teams find convenient, be reindexed in place when the office is quiet and be called directly by product applications, with removal treated as one more update.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this lets the platform team own engine, clusters, indexer framework, contract and capacity while marketplaces own schemas, analyzers and ranking; runs two engines during a migration behind one API; and watches freshness percentiles per operation, index fields without a source, cache hit ratios at peak and cost per thousand searches, revisiting the engine on a fixed cycle with shadow traffic.
thesis.how_why: Listing search is a high-write store whose queries are mostly filters. posts.title: What Did They Mean? Query Understanding and Autocomplete
posts.question: How do you turn short, ambiguous queries into the right structured search?

know: The query-understanding pipeline from raw string to structured query (analysis per language, spelling and synonyms, query categorization, attribute extraction) and its ownership split: one vocabulary, many policies.

The confidence-to-action policy (filter, boost, suggest) with removable chips and the rule that adding an interpretation never increases results, the null-result recovery ladder, autocomplete, hybrid retrieval with its fusion methods, and the LLM query compiler with its validation step.
believe: Meaning belongs in the attribute dictionary and the taxonomy, versioned with them, not in scattered synonym files.
Embeddings and language models are layers over the structured core, not replacements for it, and need per-market evaluation and owners.
can_do: Add a query-understanding checklist (aliases, categorizer labels, evaluation sets) to a taxonomy release and test analyzers for token parity across engines.

Apply high-confidence interpretations as a filter shown as a removable chip, weaker ones as a boost and suggestion, never letting an added interpretation increase results, and recover from thin results with a defined ladder (widen the radius before broadening the category).

thesis.question: How do you turn short, ambiguous queries into the right structured search?
thesis.claim: In listing search, understanding a query mostly means compiling it into the marketplace's own categories and attribute filters: the vocabulary (aliases per language, exclusions such as 'speed pedelec') lives once in the taxonomy and attribute service, each marketplace applies interpretations by calibrated confidence (a filter shown as a removable chip at 0.85 or above at Tradeyard, a boost and suggestion below), thin results are recovered in a defined relaxation order, and dense retrieval and LLM query compilers are layers that emit the same validated filter form under the same per-market evaluation and ownership as any order-tier model.

posts.question: How should a marketplace order results so buyers find the right listing and sellers get fair exposure?

Paid listings now hold 38% of first-page positions, sessions with a contact are falling, and Monetization says the products work. Using only this chapter: what do you change, and how do you decide whether it worked?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Separate a relevance model trained on contacts, with no entitlement features, from a versioned ranking policy owned jointly by search and monetization and reviewed in the advice forum; freeze and remove the boost functions; admit paid slots only above a relevance floor, cap paid positions (for example four in the first 20, slots and bumps together), bound bumps in relevance sort, limit listings per seller and reserve exploration positions for new listings; emit reason codes and delivery events and generate the ranking-parameters description from the policy file. Test with randomization by category and region cluster, judged on sessions with a contact, new-listing contacts and contacts per paid listing as well as revenue per search; reposition the paid product as guaranteed prominence in relevant searches.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Tradeyard's top-listing boost that ate relevance; ranking as prominence, not a sort; model, policy layer and ranking log; learning to rank; the ranking policy's rules: the default sort and bumps, exploration slots and per-seller caps; blending paid visibility with organic results; transparency as a regulated function; evaluating ranking changes; Ranking policy v1; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: published ranking work of marketplaces such as Airbnb and Etsy, EU law (P2B Regulation, Omnibus Directive) and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How should a marketplace order results so buyers find the right listing and sellers get fair exposure?
thesis.claim: The order of a listing results page should come from two separately owned parts: a relevance model trained on contacts that never sees what a seller paid, and a versioned ranking policy that applies freshness, paid products, seller diversity and exploration under a relevance floor and a cap on paid positions (at most four paid listings in the first 20 at Tradeyard), emits delivery events billing can read and reason codes from which the legally required description of ranking parameters is generated, and is judged on contacts and seller-side guardrails rather than on clicks or revenue per search.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of expressing paid visibility as reserved slots and score multipliers in engine boost functions, each A/B tested on revenue per search, on the grounds that sellers buy them because they work and that the revenue funds the free listings that keep the marketplace liquid.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this sets a group standard that relevance models consume no entitlements, gives each brand a ranking council that owns the primary metric, guardrails and policy file, shares the ranking service, log schema, evaluation tooling and transparency generator while models and policy values stay per brand, and watches the paid share of first-page positions, the new-listing first-contact rate and delivery against sold for every paid product.
thesis.how_why: Tradeyard's ranking was deposited in five boost layers between 2016 and 2025, each tested on revenue alone: paid listings rose from 12% to 38% of first-page positions, almost a third of them below median organic relevance, sessions with a contact fell from 10.6% to 9.4% and new private listings without a contact in 48 hours rose from 24% to 33%. Ranking policy v1, tested from 6 September to 17 October 2027, cut the paid share to 17%, raised sessions with a contact by 5.3% and contacts per top listing sold by 21% at a 2.5% cost in VAS revenue per search, because no paid listing was shown below the relevance floor and each reached buyers whose query it matched.

role.contribution: Makes the order of results an owned, versioned policy separate from the relevance model, and defines the candidate, re-ranking, exposure and logging machinery the later surfaces reuse.

transition_in.carries_over: Query understanding's output, the structured query and the candidates it retrieves, which says what the engine finds but not the order in which buyers see it.
transition_in.introduces: Ordering those candidates as a negotiation between relevance, freshness, seller fairness and paid visibility, settled by a relevance model and a versioned policy.

posts.title: Recommendations for Inventory That Disappears
posts.question: How do you recommend items that may be sold tomorrow?

know: The recommendation surfaces of a listing marketplace and why churn breaks the usual recommender: every listing is a cold-start problem and may disappear before the buyer clicks.

The generate, filter, re-rank, apply-policy architecture; events and serving-time checks; cold start for new listings, new users and new markets; feedback loops and exposure; evaluation by contacts and coverage; consent and the non-profiling option for very large platforms.
believe: Churn changes a recommender's plumbing more than its algorithms, and a nightly batch job over a catalog that changes by the hour produces Ghost Inventory.
Carousel click-through is the wrong success metric; contacts and inventory coverage are the right ones.
can_do: Design a recommendation pipeline whose candidate indices take inserts and deletes from listing events and whose single serving-time filter reads the shared status read model.
Set an exposure policy (dealer concentration cap, exploration slot) and decide what a group shares for recommendations and what each brand keeps.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a carousel that shows sold items and ignores new ones, the reader redesigns it and names the metric that decides success.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your 'similar vehicles' carousel is a nightly co-view job. It starts 7% of leads, but 41% of new listings get no carousel impression in their first three days and about 4% of clicks land on sold cars. Using only this chapter: how do you rebuild it, and by what metric do you judge the rebuild?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Several candidate sources (attribute similarity over the search index, embeddings with a content tower so new cars get vectors at once, frequently recomputed co-contact neighbors, fresh listings nearby) kept current by listing events within a minute; one serving-time filter on the shared status read model plus trust, duplicate and already-contacted rules; a re-ranker trained on leads with position logged; a policy capping cars per dealer group and reserving an exploration slot for new listings. Judge it on leads and inventory coverage, not click-through, which may fall slightly as the carousel shows newer, comparable cars; and close the sale-to-removal gap at the source (a mark-as-sold event, a fast status delta in the supply contract).

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The sold Golf that kept being recommended at Motorvane; recommendation surfaces; why listings break the usual recommender; methods under churn; generate, filter, re-rank, apply policy; events and serving-time checks; cold start in three forms; feedback loops and exposure; evaluation; privacy, consent and regulation; the Motorvane rebuild; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: published marketplace recommender work (Airbnb listing embeddings and others), EU regulation and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How do you recommend items that may be sold tomorrow?
thesis.claim: Recommending inventory that may be sold tomorrow depends on plumbing more than on modeling: several candidate sources, each one index lookup, including content and image features that give a listing a place before anyone has viewed it, feed candidate indices that listing events update within a minute; one serving-time filter on the shared status read model removes unavailable, ineligible and unconsented items; a re-ranker with an exposure policy (a cap per dealer group, an exploration slot for new listings) is judged on contacts and inventory coverage rather than click-through; and every surface has a non-personalized mode that serves a complete list when personalization is unavailable or not consented to.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice, inherited from retail, of building recommendations as a nightly collaborative-filtering batch job (co-views or co-purchases written to a key-value store) and judging it on carousel click-through.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this shares the status read model and listing event stream, candidate-serving infrastructure with real-time upserts, deletes and filtered search, the recommendation log and evaluation tooling and consent propagation across brands, keeps models, source weights and policy values per brand, and watches contacts on unavailable listings by surface, new-listing exposure within 72 hours, weekly coverage and seller concentration.
thesis.how_why: Motorvane's 2020 co-view carousel could recommend only cars someone had already viewed alongside another: 41% of new listings got no carousel impression in their first 72 hours although the carousel started 7% of leads, 3.8% of clicks landed on sold or removed cars, and the sold Essen Golf stayed in carousels until the next nightly run. The rebuild (four candidate sources, one filter, a GBDT re-ranker, at most two cars per dealer group in ten) raised carousel-started leads by 16% relative, cut new listings without an impression to 8% and clicks on unavailable cars to 0.3%, while click-through fell 4%.

role.contribution: Extends the read-model and owned-order arguments to ranking without a query, where churn makes availability and cold start the design problem.

transition_in.carries_over: Ranking's machinery (candidate generation, re-ranking, exposure policy and position-corrected logging), which orders what a buyer asked for.
transition_in.introduces: Surfaces with no query to anchor relevance, such as similar listings and home feeds, where every listing is a cold start and may be gone before the buyer clicks.

posts.title: Searching by Place: Map, Polygon and Commute Search
posts.question: How do you build location-centric discovery for verticals where place is the main filter?

know: The five ways buyers say 'here' (named area, radius, viewport, drawn shape, commute) and why a map is a different product from a list: many small viewport queries, clusters and counts, its own ranking and evaluation.
The geo query compiler and its primitives, the three clustering approaches, polygon normalization, isochrones versus post-retrieval travel times, neighborhood data, and caching at the peak.
believe: The compiler, not the client, owns the translation of a gesture into a query, so caching, privacy and cost rules apply everywhere.
Precision, privacy and routing cost are design inputs: pins come from the public point, one canonical property is one pin, and the routing provider's pricing decides how commute search runs.
can_do: Specify a geo query compiler with vertex caps, snapping and precision rules configured per brand, and budget map requests separately in capacity planning.
Decide on a routing provider from a forecast of peak isochrone and matrix volumes.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given slow drawn-area queries, stacked pins and a commute-search request, the reader states the design for each.
acceptance_criteria.probe: At your property portal, drawn-area searches arrive as raw finger traces of hundreds or thousands of vertices and take almost two seconds at peak; agencies complain that one flat they list jointly shows as three stacked pins; and product wants '30 minutes by public transport' search for spring. Using only this chapter: what do you build, and how do you choose the routing provider?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A geo query compiler owned by the search platform, in front of the engine, that repairs and simplifies drawn polygons under a vertex cap, snaps viewports to cached tiles and turns named areas into place-ID filters; pins and clusters computed from the public point, never the exact one, and counted per canonical property, so the jointly listed flat is one pin with several offers; commute search as cached isochrones keyed by a snapped origin plus travel-time matrices for pins on screen. Choose routing from a forecast of peak isochrone and matrix volumes against the provider's pricing and license: a per-request price list grows with every campaign, a fixed license or self-hosted engine turns it into capacity planning.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Hearthly's polygon problem in Lyon; five ways to say 'here'; the map as a different product; a geo query compiler in front of the engine; drawn polygons; clustering; commute search with isochrones and travel times; neighborhood data; performance and caching at the peak; the Lyon apartment on the map; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: published work of Airbnb, Zillow and other portals, routing and engine documentation and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How do you build location-centric discovery for verticals where place is the main filter?
thesis.claim: Where place is the main filter, map search should be built as its own product over one geo query compiler, owned by the search platform and configured by brands, that turns named areas, drawn shapes, commutes and viewports into a few cacheable primitives (place-ID filters, simplified polygons, isochrones or post-retrieval travel times, tile-aligned boxes); pins and clusters are computed from each listing's public point and counted per canonical property; map traffic is budgeted, ranked and evaluated separately from lists; and commute search is costed from a forecast of peak isochrone and matrix volumes, because at hundreds of isochrones per second a per-request price grows with every campaign while a fixed license or a self-hosted engine turns the cost into capacity planning.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of treating location as one filter among many (a radius around a postcode), letting each client build its own geo queries from raw gestures, plotting the ranked list as pins, and choosing a routing provider by its feature list.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this shares the geo primitives, compiler, place and boundary service, isochrone service and tile cache while brands keep the map experience, writes the precision rule as a platform invariant signed off by the data protection officer, puts entity resolution's quality on the search platform's dashboard, budgets map requests rather than searches, and decides routing on a forecast of peak isochrone and matrix volumes.
thesis.how_why: At Hearthly France 61% of sessions open the map and 17% draw an area; about 2,700 of 4,200 peak requests per second are map requests; raw traces arrive with a median of 146 vertices and more than 2,000 at most, giving polygon queries a 1.8-second p99 against 210 ms for list queries over the same city; and a Lyon flat listed by three agencies showed as three stacked pins. In the worked example the compiler simplifies a 181-vertex trace to 27 vertices and shows the flat as one pin with three offers; Airbnb reports that maps carry about 80% of its search interactions and that list metrics misjudge them; and peak commute load in the low hundreds of isochrones and tens of thousands of matrix elements per second moves Hearthly to a fixed-license matrix provider and self-hosted isochrones.

role.contribution: Applies the compile-into-structure claim to place, and shows that a map surface needs its own budget, ranking and evaluation over shared geo machinery.

transition_in.carries_over: Recommendations' principles (content first, availability always, measurement on matches rather than clicks) and its lesson that a surface without a typed query still needs its own ranking and evaluation.
transition_in.introduces: The map, where the result set is scoped by place and displayed as pins and clusters, and the geo query compiler that turns gestures into query primitives.

posts.title: Tell Me When It Appears: Saved Searches and Alerts
posts.question: How do you notify millions of users within minutes when a matching listing appears?

know: Saved searches as persisted, normalized queries with an owner, a notification policy and a lifecycle; percolation versus batch re-querying; alert fan-out with deduplication, quotas and bursts.

The rule of notifying on entering the match set, send-time re-checks for digests, the alert metrics (latency, alert-to-contact, ghost-alert, unsubscribe and dormant rates), the risk gate in front of the matcher, saved-search migration through taxonomy changes, and consent and retention.
believe: Alerts are a liquidity lever and a trust surface at once: they shorten time to contact and amplify whatever they carry, fraud included.
A saved search is user data that must survive taxonomy changes and model upgrades, and alerts are judged by contacts, never by sends.
can_do: Size a matcher by candidates per event and choose between percolation and re-querying for a latency target.
Design the saved-search service, notification orchestrator, risk gate and migration plan for a group, and put any widening of saved-search semantics through capacity review.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a cron-based alert system with stale digests and a fraud wave carried by alerts, the reader states the target design and its metrics.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your instant alerts run as a ten-minute cron job with a 23-minute p95 on Sunday evenings; digests assembled in the afternoon still advertise listings sold that evening; and a wave of fake rentals reached tens of thousands of renters through alerts before takedown. Using only this chapter: what do you build, and how do you know it works?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A saved-search service storing normalized queries as system of record, with percolator indices rebuilt from it, matching each new or changed listing from the event stream (reverse search) and alerting only when a listing enters a match set; a notification orchestrator with caps, quiet hours and deduplication; send-time availability re-checks for digests and retraction of removed listings from pending notifications; a risk gate owned by trust and safety that keeps risky listings not alertable until reviewed, with a stricter threshold in rentals and a short hold for new accounts' first listings. Measure alert latency from searchable to provider (for example 5 minutes p95), alert-to-contact rate, ghost-alert rate, unsubscribes and dormant share, not alerts sent.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Femke's bike, 312 saved searches and Tradeyard's ten-minute cron; saved searches, match sets and alerts; percolation versus re-querying; a saved-search store with rebuildable percolators; fan-out; channels and digests; sizing the matcher for Veldmark; alerts as a liquidity lever; the risk gate; saved searches through taxonomy changes; consent and retention; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions; then the hand-off to trust. Evidence: published designs of Rightmove and Homegate (percolators), engine documentation, trade press and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

The chapter's last section performs the part's closing: it shows how the six surfaces fit together, answers the part opening's three questions for discovery as a whole and hands off to Part V through the risk alerts carry.

thesis.question: How do you notify millions of users within minutes when a matching listing appears?
thesis.claim: Saved searches should be a system of record of normalized queries, in the same format as the search API and the geo query compiler, from which percolator indices are rebuilt; every new or changed listing is matched against them as reverse search, and an alert fires only when a listing enters a match set and passes a risk gate owned by trust and safety, with a send-time re-check for anything delivered later than it was computed and a match ledger that survives taxonomy migrations; and the service is held to latency (5 minutes p95 from searchable to provider at Veldmark), alert-to-contact and ghost-alert targets, not to the number of alerts sent.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of running alerts as a periodic cron job that re-queries recent listings against saved searches in a relational table, assembling digests hours before they are sent, counting notifications sent as success, and dropping or resetting saved searches when the taxonomy changes.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this makes the saved-search store, matcher, notification orchestrator and consent policy group platforms while brands keep alert content and design, reports alert latency and ghost-alert rate weekly as platform SLOs, puts every widening of saved-search semantics through capacity review, makes saved-search migration part of every taxonomy and gazetteer change, and lets trust and safety govern alertability as a derived listing state.
thesis.how_why: Femke's €240 bike matched 312 saved searches and drew its first contact from an alert seven minutes after it became searchable, yet 214 digest e-mails assembled from a replica at 17:30 still featured it at 07:00 after its sale; Tradeyard's ten-minute cron ran at a 23-minute p95 on Sunday evenings and about 4% of digest items were no longer available. Matching is costly by candidates per event, not by events: at a peak of 80 events per second and 50,000 candidates each the percolator evaluates up to 4 million stored queries per second, which dormancy pausing and place pre-filters reduce. And 180 fake Eixample rentals produced about 41,000 alerts and about €71,000 in losses before takedown, which is why risky listings stay not alertable until a review clears them.

role.contribution: Turns a search into standing demand that reuses every earlier surface, and performs the part's closing: discovery now reaches motivated buyers within minutes, which is why trust must gate it.

transition_in.carries_over: Map search's saved draw-your-area search, stored as a normalized polygon and isochrone parameters, and the finding that a buyer can only find what is listed at the moment they search.
transition_in.introduces: What is listed afterwards: the saved search as standing demand, matched by reverse search against every new or changed listing and delivered as alerts within minutes.

parts.title: Part V — TRUST: Keeping the Marketplace Safe

know: Trust and safety as five functions (policy, detection, decision, enforcement, review and redress) plus measurement, joined by one decision record; enforcement as an event every consumer acknowledges; moderation mode set per risk tier; metrics of harm (sampled prevalence, time to action, precision, overturn rate) rather than activity.

The classifieds fraud threat model (authorized push payment fraud that closes off the platform), the risk scoring service with its real-time and streaming paths, rules and models, the identity graph and actor-level scoring, step-up friction chosen by a cost model, message controls and the label loop.

Identity as expiring, revocable claims from which levels and badges are derived; step-up at risky actions; passkeys, risk-based authentication and recovery against account takeover; a group identity with brand profiles and pairwise identifiers.

How features decide which laws apply, and the five components (obligation register, decision record and evidence store, trader registry, disclosure surfaces, reporting views) that serve the DSA, P2B and Omnibus rules, GDPR, DAC7 and vertical rules.
believe: Trust and safety is a platform capability beneath the brands, not a team with a queue per brand: share the machinery, evidence and lawful hashed signals; keep policy content, thresholds and vertical detectors local.
Fraud is stopped at its setup, before the money leaves the platform, by scoring actors as well as items and by friction in proportion to risk, not by blocking everything suspicious.
Regulation asks for a few records built once, and every regulated number must be computable again from the event log.
can_do: Say, for any enforcement decision, who made it, under which policy version, where it propagated and how to prove all three a year later.

Decide which trust capabilities a group shares (decision service, enforcement events, case tooling, evidence store, statement-of-reasons service, rule runtime, risk scoring service, identity service, compliance components) and which each brand keeps (policy overlays, thresholds, reviewers, vertical detectors).
Review a planned transaction or payment feature for the identity levels, fraud controls and regulatory perimeter it brings with it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
A reader who has read only Part V can assign five trust incidents to the chapter whose design owns each and name the control that design applies.
acceptance_criteria.probe: In one quarter at a marketplace group: a listing removed for fraud at 09:00 still appears in the 10:00 alert digest and its seller's payout goes out; 26 new accounts post 180 cheap rentals whose photos match other agencies' listings, while photo matches wait in a 'possible duplicates' queue and price anomalies in another; a dealer whose business closed two years ago still shows a 'verified' badge; the regulator asks you to reproduce last year's count of listing removals and five exporters give different numbers; and product wants to launch in-platform payments next quarter. Using only Part V, which chapter's design owns each, and what does it do?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Trust-and-safety architecture: the decision service emits an EnforcementApplied event that every consumer (alerts, recommendations, payments and the rest) applies and acknowledges, a propagation monitor tracks the last acknowledgement, and the action is not done until then. Fraud prevention: a photo match with an unrelated seller is a fraud signal combined with price, account age and verification into one risk score; the identity graph links the accounts through devices and IBANs, one case covers the cluster and its listings are held at the gate; rules are shadow-tested in hours. Identity and verification: business claims expire and are re-checked (continuous KYB), and a badge states only what was checked and lapses with its claim. Marketplace regulation: one decision record feeds statements of reasons and reports, and every reported number is a saved, versioned query over immutable events; in-platform payments move the marketplace into DAC7 and trader traceability, so the feature is a regulatory decision and the DAC7 pipeline aggregates from the payment ledger.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The last section of marketplace-regulation performs the part's closing: it shows how the decision record, risk scores, identity claims and the law's five components fit together, says why that matters for Part VI, and returns to the part opening's test of who decided, under which policy version, where it propagated and how to prove it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Does the final section of marketplace-regulation state something about Part V that no single chapter states, say why it matters for Part VI, and return to the question the part introduction ends on?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A synthesis that the part's chapters produce and consume the same few records (decision record, risk scores and actor clusters, identity claims and trader record, reports computed from the event log); a so-what about messaging, payments and paid placements in Part VI; an explicit return to the part introduction's test (who made a decision, under which policy version, where it propagated, how to prove it a year later).

thesis.question: How does a marketplace group keep contact between strangers safe, and prove to a regulator months later what it did?
thesis.claim: Trust in a marketplace group should be built as one shared platform beneath the brands rather than a moderation queue per brand: policy, detection, decision, enforcement and review are separate components joined by one decision record that a single decision service writes and every consumer from search to payments must acknowledge; fraud is stopped at its setup, before the money leaves by bank transfer, by one risk scoring service that scores linked actors as well as items and answers risk with friction set by a cost model; identity is a set of expiring claims requested at the moment of risk under one group login that a sold brand can be cut out of; and the DSA, DAC7, consumer and vertical rules are met by five compliance components built once (obligation register, decision record and evidence store, trader registry, disclosure surfaces, reporting views), with every regulated number computable again from the event log, while policy content, thresholds and vertical detectors stay with each brand.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of treating trust and safety as operations: a review queue per brand attached to insertion, fraud judged listing by listing, identity checked once at registration or by a document upload after a fraud wave, and each law met by a per-country project or exporter when its deadline arrives; or, at the other extreme, one central team of moderators with one policy for the whole group.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this funds the decision service, the enforcement event contract, the risk scoring service, the identity service and the compliance components as group platform ahead of brand features; lets the Data Protection Officer decide which signals may cross brands; leaves thresholds and policy overlays to brands within group guardrails; reviews every payment or checkout feature as a trust and regulatory decision; and reports sampled prevalence of fraudulent listings by brand and time from first fraudulent listing to cluster takedown, not removal counts.
thesis.how_why: Veldmark's 2027 incidents each failed between stacks, not inside one. On 7 March a phishing link reached Femke sixteen minutes after her first buyer contact; Tradeyard NL suspended the account seven minutes after her report, but its phone number had a Motorvane account no one could see, Tradeyard Belgium received the new rule days later and Poland and Portugal never did. In July 26 accounts posted 180 fake Barcelona rentals and 63 people lost about €71,000 over about twelve and a half days, while photo and price signals sat in separate queues from day one. And the 2026 DSA transparency reports, drawn from five statement-of-reasons exporters that counted differently, could not be produced again. Each repair joins signals, decisions or records that the brands kept apart.

supporting_claims.claim: Trust and safety is five functions (policy, detection, decision, enforcement, review and redress) plus measurement, built as separate components: policies are versioned reference data, one decision service is the only writer of decision records, the moderation mode is set per risk tier rather than chosen once, an enforcement action (demotion included) is done only when every consumer has acknowledged its EnforcementApplied event, and the platform is judged on sampled prevalence, time to action, precision and appeal overturn rate rather than removal counts.

A group shares the trust machinery beneath its brands (decision service, enforcement events, case tooling, evidence store, statement-of-reasons service, rule runtime, risk scoring service and identity graph, one login with brand profiles and pairwise identifiers) and only those cross-brand signals the Data Protection Officer approves, such as hashed block lists of fraud-terminated accounts, while policy content, thresholds, reviewers and vertical detectors stay with each brand and any brand can still be separated.

Classifieds fraud is mostly authorized push payment fraud that closes off the platform, so controls act before the payment: one risk scoring service scores actors linked in an identity graph as well as items within the latency of a user action, combined rules are backtested and shadowed before rollout, friction thresholds come from an explicit cost model whose inputs the business owns, message links are checked before delivery, and labels from victims, banks, reviewers and appeals reach the models within days.

Identity is a set of separate, expiring and revocable claims (contactability, authentication strength, proof of person, proof of business) from which levels and badges are derived; a level is required at the moment of risk (contact, rental publication, payout, trading) rather than at registration, recovery is held to the strength of login, and a badge states only what was checked.

Features decide which laws apply, so every payment, checkout or shipping feature is a regulatory decision; the obligations of the DSA, P2B and Omnibus rules, GDPR, DAC7 and vertical rules ask for five components built once (obligation register, decision record and evidence store, trader and business registry, disclosure surfaces, reporting views), with country differences as configuration and every regulated number a saved, versioned query over immutable events.

role.contribution: Supplies the guarantee that the matches the earlier parts produce are safe, and the decisions every other stage must obey.

additional_patterns.applies_to: trust-and-safety-architecture to identity-and-verification: the platform and its decision record, then the most demanding detector it hosts (fraud scoring), then the strongest friction that detector asks for (identity checks)

flow.rationale: Each chapter plugs into what the one before it built, and the last reads the records all of them produce. Trust-and-safety architecture comes first because it builds the decision service, the decision record, enforcement propagation and appeals, and leaves detection as a slot; placed after fraud prevention, risk scores would be computed with no decision service to turn them into enforcement, no appeals to label them and no propagation path to make them take effect. Fraud prevention follows because it fills that slot with the most demanding detector and ends on the strongest friction it can apply, an identity check; placed after identity, the identity levels would be required at 'moments of risk' before the reader has met the risk scores and cost model that decide when to step up, and the Barcelona policy in identity-and-verification would cite a detection story not yet told. Identity precedes regulation because the business registry and the trader record built on it, which DSA traceability, P2B and DAC7 read, are designed there; placed first, regulation would demand a decision record and a trader registry the reader has not seen designed, and would read as a list of laws rather than as views over existing components; regulation does not rebuild the decision record or the registry, it adds the obligation register, disclosure surfaces and reporting views over them. Regulation comes last also because it is where Part VI's threads begin: payments move the legal perimeter into DAC7, labels govern paid placements, and trader records feed billing.

hook.content: Part IV built surfaces that put listings in front of buyers within seconds. Fraudsters exploit that speed: a fake rental that reaches saved searches in minutes reaches the most motivated victims first.

opening.bridge: From Part IV's discovery surfaces, which put strangers in contact within minutes, to the trust that makes that contact safe, and to the group that starts 2027 with four trust-and-safety stacks, four identity systems and five sources of statements of reasons that cannot share a signal.
opening.roadmap: Four chapters: trust and safety as a platform with one decision record and enforcement path, fraud prevention by scoring actors and graduated friction, identity requested at the moment of risk under one group login, and regulation turned into a few reusable components; framed by Veldmark's two 2027 incidents (the 7 March phishing link and the July Barcelona fake-rental ring) and its four decisions (Veldmark ID, the obligation register, the shared trust-and-safety platform, first-contact friction); ending on the test that for any enforcement decision the reader can say who made it, under which policy version, where it propagated and how to prove all three a year later.

closing.synthesis: The four chapters produce and read the same few records: the decision record that trust-and-safety architecture makes the single output of moderation, the risk scores and actor clusters that fraud prevention feeds into it, the identity claims and trader record that identity and verification keeps, and the five components through which the law asks for exactly these records as evidence. Trust is one platform because its records are shared, not because its people are.
closing.so_what: Every revenue line in Part VI steps onto this platform: messaging is where scams close and where identity levels gate contact, in-platform payments move the marketplace into DAC7 and trader traceability, and paid placements need the labels and ranking disclosures regulation specifies; a group that built trust as four stacks pays for each of those again.
closing.callback: The part introduction's closing test: for any enforcement decision, who made it, under which policy version, where it propagated, and how you would prove all three a year later.

takeaway.content: Review every transaction feature as a trust and regulatory decision before it is a product decision; Part VI begins with messaging-and-leads, the moment a buyer decides to contact a seller.

transition_in.carries_over: Part IV's discovery surfaces, which put a new listing in front of its most motivated buyers within minutes, and saved-searches-and-alerts' closing warning that alerts amplify whatever they carry, as the 180 fake Eixample rentals and their 41,000 alerts showed.
transition_in.introduces: The risk that contact between strangers carries, and the trust platform whose decisions publication, search, alerts and messaging must obey.
