posts.title: Trust and Safety as a Platform
posts.question: How should trust and safety be architected across listings, users, messages and transactions?

know: The five functions of trust and safety (policy, detection, decision, enforcement, review and redress) plus measurement, the speed at which each changes and how each fails; policies as versioned reference data.

The moderation pipeline: synchronous gate and asynchronous path, risk-tiered moderation modes, human review queues and the random sample, LLMs for the grey zone; the enforcement ladder and its propagation to every consumer; notice and action, case management, appeals and statements of reasons as a by-product.
The trust-and-safety metrics (prevalence, time to action, precision, recall, overturn rate, report rate, reviewer agreement) and how each misleads.
believe: A removal is not finished when the listing's status changes; it is finished when the last consumer has acknowledged it.
Trust and safety pays to share across brands from the first year, but only the machinery, evidence and lawful signals; policy judgement stays local.
can_do: Draw the trust-and-safety components and their interfaces, with one decision service as the only writer of decision records.
Defend a risk-tiered moderation design instead of a choice between pre- and post-moderation, and say what must happen in every system when a listing or account is restricted.
Decide which trust-and-safety components a group shares and which each brand keeps.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an incomplete removal and an undeclared demotion practice, the reader names what is missing and what the design does.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A fraudulent listing removed at 09:00 still appears in a 10:00 alert digest and in a similar-items carousel, its seller's open payout goes out, and the ranking team has been quietly demoting suspected scams for months. Using only this chapter: what is missing, and what does the design do?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Enforcement is an EnforcementApplied event from the decision service that every consumer applies idempotently and acknowledges: alerts drop queued notifications and exclude the listing from digests, recommendations evict it, payments hold or freeze per policy; a propagation monitor tracks time to the last acknowledgement, and the removal is not done until then. Demotion is a restriction under Article 17 of the DSA, so it must go through the decision service with a decision record and a statement of reasons.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The four-stacks history and the question 'what did we remove, why, and did it disappear'; the Veldmark phishing incident and the group's four stacks; the five functions and policies as data; the moderation pipeline with the public practice behind it, modes, human review and LLMs; enforcement and its propagation; intake, cases, appeals and statements of reasons; metrics; what a group shares and how verticals differ; trade-offs, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: the DSA, public engineering sources (Meta's Sigma, Stripe Radar, OLX), the Which? 2024 test, the 2015 leboncoin ruling and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How should trust and safety be architected across listings, users, messages and transactions?
thesis.claim: Trust and safety should be built as five separately owned functions (policy, detection, decision, enforcement, review and redress) plus measurement, joined by one decision record that a single decision service writes: policies are versioned reference data that every rule, model, reviewer guideline and notice cites; the moderation mode is set per risk tier of category, seller and listing rather than chosen once; an enforcement action, demotion included, is done only when every consumer (search, alerts, recommendations, messaging, SEO pages, ads, payments, partner feeds) has acknowledged its EnforcementApplied event; the platform is judged on sampled prevalence, time to action, precision and appeal overturn rate rather than removal counts; and a group shares this machinery and lawful hashed block lists while each brand keeps its policy overlays, thresholds, reviewers and vertical detectors.
thesis.disputed_by: The common view that trust and safety is an operations function: a review queue attached to insertion, staffed per brand or outsourced, measured by items reviewed and listings removed, with a removal finished once the listing's status changes, and with sharing across a group meaning centralized moderators and one policy.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this makes the decision record schema and the single-writer rule a group decision, sets propagation targets per consumer and watches p95 and worst case, lets the Data Protection Officer decide which signals cross brands, leaves risk tiers and thresholds to marketplace general managers within group guardrails, and puts sampled prevalence of fraudulent listings by brand, next to time to action on fraud reports, in front of the board.
thesis.how_why: On 7 March 2027 Tradeyard NL suspended a phishing account seven minutes after Femke's report, yet its phone number also had a Motorvane account no one could see, Tradeyard Belgium received the new rule on Wednesday, Poland and Portugal never did, and the sellers it had already contacted got no warning: four stacks with 210 moderators, three appeal processes and five ways of producing statements of reasons could not share a signal. A blind sample of 4,000 Tradeyard NL listings a week found about 0.6% violating policy against the 0.2% removal counts suggested. The shared platform, live for Tradeyard NL and BE in November 2027, targets 96% automation from 94%, a median time to action on fraud reports under 30 minutes from 3 hours 10 minutes, and an alert when the overturn rate of a policy exceeds 10%.

role.contribution: Builds the platform the rest of the part plugs into, the decision service, decision record, enforcement propagation, appeals and metrics, and sets out which of it a group shares.

transition_in.carries_over: The part introduction's argument that trust is a platform capability, not a team with a queue, and its picture of Veldmark's four trust-and-safety stacks that cannot share a signal.
transition_in.introduces: The platform itself: five functions, one decision service and record, enforcement that reaches every consumer, cases and appeals, metrics of harm, and the split between shared machinery and local policy.

posts.title: Scams, Fakes and Account Takeovers: Fraud Prevention for Listings
posts.question: How do marketplaces detect and stop fraud, from fake listings to payment scams?

know: The classifieds threat model: authorized push payment fraud that is set up on the platform and closes off it, a fraud typology with dated public evidence, and a signal taxonomy judged by availability, cost of evasion and cost to genuine users.

The risk scoring service: real-time and streaming paths, a feature store only when real-time behavioral features need one, rules and models with a backtest-shadow-rollout lifecycle, the identity graph and actor-level scoring.
Step-up friction and its cost model, message-level fraud controls, late and biased labels, adversarial adaptation, and collaboration with banks and police.
believe: A fake listing looks plausible one at a time; the fraud is visible when listings, accounts, devices, payment accounts and photos are linked and scored together.
Blocking everything suspicious costs liquidity; friction in proportion to risk, at a threshold chosen by cost, costs genuine users little and fraudsters a lot.
can_do: Design a risk scoring service that insertion, messaging, login and payout call, with actor-level scoring and a rule lifecycle.
Choose a friction threshold from an explicit cost model and name who owns each input.
Say which components would have turned the Barcelona ring's day-one signals into day-one action.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given the first evening of a fake-rental ring, the reader names what should happen and when.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A new account posts a flat at 35% below comparable rents with a photo that matches another agency's listing; that evening two more new accounts on the same device post similar flats. Your photo matches go to a 'possible duplicates' queue and price anomalies to a separate low-priority queue. Using only this chapter: what should happen, and when?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A photo match with an unrelated, non-agency seller is a fraud signal sent to risk scoring, not a duplicate; one listing risk score combines photo reuse, price, account age and lister verification; the identity graph links the accounts through the shared device at creation and cluster risk raises every member's score; reviewers get one case for the cluster; the remaining listings are held at the gate that evening; analysts write and shadow-test a combined rule in hours.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The off-platform nature of classifieds fraud and the three terms the chapter owns (fraud signal, risk score, step-up friction); the Barcelona ring; the threat model and typology; vertical differences; signals including duplicate photos; the risk scoring service with real-time and batch paths, rules and models, actor scoring; step-up friction with a threshold example; messaging controls; labels and adaptation; banks and police; back to Barcelona; trade-offs, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: UK Finance, OLX, Which?, Meta, Stripe Radar and Airbnb public sources, and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How do marketplaces detect and stop fraud, from fake listings to payment scams?
thesis.claim: Because classifieds fraud is mostly authorized push payment fraud that closes off the platform, by bank transfer after a conversation, a marketplace should stop it at the setup: one risk scoring service, called by insertion, messaging, login and payout within the latency of the action, combines weak signals (reused photos, prices far below market, new accounts, shared devices and IBANs) and scores actors linked in an identity graph as well as items; combined rules are backtested and shadowed before rollout; risk is answered with step-up friction at the threshold an explicit cost model chooses, with the cost of a lost genuine user owned by the general manager; links and payment requests in messages are checked before delivery; and labels from victims, banks, reviewers and appeals reach the models within days.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that classifieds fraud is the payment provider's and the bank's problem, or that the answer is a better classifier judging each listing on its own, with suspicious items blocked outright and fraud queues worked in the order reports arrive.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this builds one risk scoring service with a contract for every caller instead of scoring in each team, puts the identity graph and its cross-brand data flows under the Data Protection Officer's approval, buys signals but owns decisions and labels, has general managers own the cost of a lost genuine user, and tracks time from first fraudulent listing to cluster takedown in hours rather than days.
thesis.how_why: The Barcelona ring's signals existed on day one: photo matches to unrelated sellers were queued as possible duplicates, prices about 35% below market sat in a separate low-priority queue, and the 26 accounts looked unrelated, so 180 fake rentals ran from 1 to 13 July 2027 and 63 people lost about €71,000, most of it paid between 5 and 12 July. A rule combining a photo match with an unrelated seller, rent at least 25% below the district estimate, an account younger than 30 days and a lister that is not a verified agency stopped the ring in an afternoon, twelve days in. Tradeyard's first-contact friction shows the threshold arithmetic: a message-risk threshold of 0.5 gave a weekly cost of about €171,500 against €360,000 with no friction, lower than both the stricter 0.7 and the looser 0.3.

role.contribution: Fills the platform's detection slot with the most demanding detector, risk scoring of actors against adaptive adversaries, and makes the case for scoring and labels shared across brands.

transition_in.carries_over: Trust-and-safety-architecture's platform, which deliberately left detection as a slot that detectors plug into, and its closing point that the most demanding detectors face people who study the platform and adapt within days.
transition_in.introduces: That adversary and the detector built for it: the classifieds threat model, fraud signals, the risk scoring service with actor-level scoring, step-up friction and the Barcelona fake-rental ring.

posts.title: Who Is on the Other Side? Identity and Verification
posts.question: How much should a marketplace know about its users, and how does it verify it?

know: Proofing, authentication and business verification as separate axes in the NIST SP 800-63-4 vocabulary; identity levels (person and business ladders) derived from claims; KYB; verified badges as statements to the other side.

The identity service and its neighbors, the claim record (type, method, source, attributes, assurance, expiry, status) and its lifecycle; passkeys, risk-based authentication, recovery and pre-hijacking; proofing methods including bank eIDs and the EU Digital Identity Wallet with its actual obligations.
The group identity options (per-brand, shared with one profile, shared with brand profiles and pairwise identifiers, federation broker) and why separability matters.
believe: The right amount of identity depends on what the user is about to do; asking for everything at the door or nothing at all both fail.
A badge that outlives its claim is a false statement, and a group identity that cannot be cut is a liability to the owners.
can_do: Design the claim contract and the level policy, and place step-up verification at specific risky actions with its cost estimated.
Name the account-takeover controls and the recovery rules that keep a strong login strong.
Choose a group identity topology and challenge a 'verified' badge that promises more than was checked.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a group with per-brand logins, a phone-number badge, one-time dealer checks and an owner asking about a sale, the reader names what to build.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your group runs a separate login per brand; its 'verified' badge means a confirmed phone number; dealers were checked once when they signed; and the owner asks what it would cost to sell one brand. Using only this chapter: what do you build?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Claims with method, source, time and expiry, from which levels and badges are derived; a badge that states only what was checked and is revoked when its claim lapses or the account's posture changes; business claims that expire and are re-checked (continuous KYB); levels required at contact, rental publication, payout and trading rather than at registration; one group identity with brand profiles, pairwise identifiers, a controller per brand and export, so a brand can be cut out with its users.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why marketplaces ask for too little and then too much, and that identity depends on the action; the Veldmark phone number on two brands and three identity stores; concepts (five words, three axes, levels, badges); the identity service, the claim contract and lifecycle; authentication and account takeover; proofing methods and the EU wallet; the group identity question with Schibsted, Veldmark ID, Barcelona, Motorvane and Femke; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: NIST, FIDO, Mercari, FINN and Schibsted public sources, EU law, and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How much should a marketplace know about its users, and how does it verify it?
thesis.claim: A marketplace should model identity as separate, expiring and revocable claims (contactability, authentication strength, proof of person, proof of business), each with a method, source, time and expiry, and derive identity levels and badges from them rather than store a 'verified' flag; it should require a level at the moment of risk (contacting a seller, publishing a rental, receiving a payout, trading) rather than at registration; hold account recovery to the strength of login, with passkeys and risk-based authentication against takeover; let a badge state only what was checked and lapse with its claim; and, in a group, run one identity service with brand profiles and pairwise identifiers so that any brand can be cut out with its users.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of asking for almost nothing at registration and then, after a fraud wave or a regulator's letter, an identity document from everyone, with one 'verified' flag, business checks done once at contract signature, and either a login per brand or one shared account and profile across the group.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this owns the claim types, levels and badge catalog centrally while brands decide which actions require which level, treats the identity service as tier-zero infrastructure, makes brand separability a requirement with an answer measured in weeks, budgets verification as a per-use cost in each policy's business case, and keeps the EU Digital Identity Wallet on the roadmap but off the critical path.
thesis.how_why: Femke's scammer was phone-verified on Tradeyard, and the same number had registered a Motorvane account three weeks earlier, because about 80 million accounts sat in three identity stores with no shared notion of a person while about 11 million people held accounts on two or more brands. None of the 26 Barcelona accounts had proved more than an e-mail address; requiring L4 of private landlords publishing rentals in Spain was estimated at about €115,000 a year and 8–12% drop-out of honest landlords, against about €71,000 lost in one ring, and makes each fake landlord cost a real, checkable identity. Motorvane's 21,400 dealers had been checked once, at signature. And Veldmark's private-equity owner may sell a brand, which only pairwise identifiers, a controller per brand and export make cheap.

role.contribution: Supplies the strongest friction fraud scoring calls for and the business registry on which regulation builds its trader record: identity as claims, levels required at moments of risk, and one group login designed to be cut.

transition_in.carries_over: Fraud-prevention's finding that every risk score is indirect evidence about who is on the other side, and that its strongest and most expensive frictions are identity checks.
transition_in.introduces: Therefore the identity question itself: how much a marketplace should know about its users, how it verifies it, what a badge promises, and how one identity serves a group of brands.

posts.title: Rules of the Marketplace: DSA, DAC7 and Vertical Regulation
posts.question: Which regulations shape marketplace architecture and how do they become system requirements?

know: The legal roles (hosting service, online platform, online marketplace, online intermediation service, reporting platform operator) and the features that trigger each; which rules reach a pure lead-generation site and which turn on contracts or payments concluded through the platform.

The DSA as system requirements (demotion and payment holds as restrictions, trader traceability as a data lifecycle, statements of reasons against the Transparency Database schema, transparency reports from the event log); ranking, advertising, price-reduction and review disclosures; GDPR retention per data class; DAC7 and its pipeline from the payment ledger; property and vehicle rules; UK and US rules in brief.
The obligation, the control and the evidence, and the five components that serve every law.
believe: Every transaction feature is a regulatory decision and should be reviewed as one.
Compliance by design, with the evidence query written with the control, costs less than compliance by project.
can_do: Map a regulation's articles to system requirements and owning components, and design a statement-of-reasons pipeline and a DAC7 pipeline.
Specify the disclosures and regulated listing attributes a marketplace needs, and set retention per data class.
Hold country differences as configuration over shared components and make every reported number reproducible.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an irreproducible regulatory figure and a planned payments launch, the reader names what is needed and what changes.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your regulator asks you to reproduce last year's count of listing removals, and your brands' exporters give different numbers; separately, product wants to launch in-platform payments in two countries next quarter. Using only this chapter: what do you need, and what changes?
acceptance_criteria.expected: One decision record that feeds statements of reasons, the Transparency Database and reports, with every reported number a saved, versioned query over immutable events; an obligation register linking each obligation to a control and an evidence query. Payments move the marketplace into DAC7 as a reporting platform operator and into trader traceability, so the launch is a regulatory decision: a DAC7 pipeline aggregates consideration from the payment ledger, flags sellers approaching the threshold early and keeps the tax profile separate from general identity claims.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Regulation now written in the vocabulary of systems design, the chapter's scope (EU first, UK and US briefly, not legal advice) and its claim that many obligations ask for a few artifacts; the five exporters and the irreproducible report; legal roles defined by features; the DSA as requirements and the statement-of-reasons pipeline; ranking, advertising and consumer transparency; GDPR; DAC7; property and vehicle rules; UK and US; compliance as architecture; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: EU legal texts in the Official Journal, the DSA Transparency Database, national rules and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: Which regulations shape marketplace architecture and how do they become system requirements?
thesis.claim: The regulations that bind a listing marketplace are triggered by its features, not by the label 'classifieds': a pure lead-generation site falls under the DSA's moderation duties, ranking transparency and platform-to-business rules but outside DAC7 until payments to sellers pass through it, and largely outside the DSA's online-marketplace duties until consumers conclude contracts with traders through it, so every payment, checkout or shipping feature is a regulatory decision; and the many obligations ask for five components built once, an obligation register with an evidence query per control, a decision record and evidence store, one trader and business registry, disclosure surfaces generated from documented parameters, and reporting views that are saved, versioned queries over immutable events and the payment ledger, with country differences held as configuration and each data class kept only as long as the law requires.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of treating regulation as legal review at the end of a project, met by a separate exporter, form or code path per law and per country when a deadline arrives, with transparency numbers assembled by hand each year and payments launched as a product decision only.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this owns the map from obligation to control to evidence while counsel interprets the law, puts regulatory review at the moment a transaction feature is proposed, funds the five components as platform rather than compliance overhead, and measures compliance like reliability: the share of restricting decisions with a statement sent and submitted, the time from decision to submission, and reports that can be produced again from the log.
thesis.how_why: Veldmark's first DSA transparency reports, due at the end of February 2027, drew on five statement-of-reasons exporters that counted differently: an edit rejected and then accepted counted once in one system and twice in another, Motorvane counted a paused dealer listing as a restriction in one quarter and not the next, and Hearthly Spain had no record of which decisions were automated, so no figure could be produced again. Tradeyard Safe Deal, 11.6 million transactions worth about €1.02 billion in 2026, brought Veldmark into DAC7, where about 21,000 of about 1.3 million paid sellers were reportable, which makes the pipeline a filter over the ledger; Motorvane and Hearthly, which only list and advertise, stay outside. Demotion and payment holds are restrictions that need statements of reasons, and energy-performance indicators are mandatory listing fields, so ranking, payments and schema teams build to the law as well.

role.contribution: Shows that the law asks for the records the earlier chapters build (the decision record, the trader record) plus three more components, and that payments move the legal perimeter, which carries Part V into Part VI.

transition_in.carries_over: Identity-and-verification's trader record, business registry, evidence trail and minimization rules, which it built partly because the law now asks marketplaces to know their traders and explain their decisions.
transition_in.introduces: Those laws themselves: the DSA, DAC7, ranking and consumer transparency and vertical rules, turned into system requirements served by five shared components.

parts.title: Part VI — MONEY: Conversion and Monetization

know: The contact path as two objects, a platform-held conversation and a commercial lead, with a synchronous message safety gate on the delivery path, a lead contract with a stable lead ID, deduplication and acknowledged delivery, and outcome feedback.

When a classifieds marketplace should take part in the transaction (four conditions per category), the payment models, and the six contexts a transactional pivot adds: order, payment edge, fees, shipping, buyer protection and disputes, and the transaction ledger with DAC7 reporting.

The ten monetization models, the unit of charge each sells and the system of record it selects, the published KPIs (ARPA, ARPR, yield per listing, take rate), and the liquidity each model spends with its guardrail metric.

The commercial core: product catalog, pricing engine, append-only entitlement ledger and billing kept apart, effects projected as explicit paid fields on the listing read model, and the sold-versus-delivered reconciliation.

Advertising as three businesses (display and native, sponsored listings, retail media) on three decision paths under one ad policy layer, with consent, header-bidding latency and first-party audiences as architecture decisions.
believe: Every revenue line spends liquidity, so each is metered against the match rate it costs, with a guardrail owned outside the team that books the revenue.
What a marketplace sells must be recorded once, in a record both the marketplace and its customer can count, and delivery must be provable line by line.
Taking part in the transaction is a per-category decision, and a checkout shipped without its ledger and dispute desk is a liability.
can_do: Say, for any paid product, which unit it charges for, what liquidity it spends and how they would prove it was delivered.
Judge a proposal for a new revenue line, a transactional pivot or an ad change by its system of record, its delivery evidence and its liquidity guardrail, not by its business case alone.

Decide which money capabilities a group shares (conversation service and safety gate, lead contract, transaction platform, catalog model and entitlement ledger, ad stack and audience service) and which each brand keeps (products, prices, contract terms, model choice, page ownership).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
A reader who has read only Part VI can assign five money incidents to the chapter whose design owns each and name the control that design applies.
acceptance_criteria.probe: In one year at a marketplace group: a private seller receives a fake 'protected payment' link in chat sixteen minutes after her first buyer contact, and a dealer's CRM shows 14 leads for a car the portal says produced 23; finance finds about €2.3 million of payment items in a clearing account that match no order, while product proposes escrow for €20,000 private car sales; the monetization team wants a new premium slot above the results and a per-lead fee for dealers; a dealer is billed overage for 13 cars that were never published; and the ad team lengthens the header-bidding timeout, earning about 4% more per page view while listing pages load half a second slower. Using only Part VI, which chapter's design owns each, and what does it do?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Messaging and leads: a synchronous safety gate on the delivery path withholds the link (a same-day domain) before the recipient sees it, and a lead contract with one creation and deduplication rule and a stable lead ID lets portal and dealer count the same leads (19, not 23 against 14). Transactions and payments: the transaction ledger receives order and money events so every amount is matched, shipped before further launches; escrow fails the four conditions (price, professional sellers), so at most a narrow design study. Monetization models: ask each proposal its unit, its system of truth, the liquidity it spends and who notices first, attach a guardrail metric with a stop condition owned outside the revenue team; the per-lead fee needs a lead ledger that counts before it bills. Products and entitlements: one append-only entitlement ledger records 150 consumptions and 13 refused publications, and billing reads it, so there is no overage line; delivery events reconcile with invoice lines. Advertising platforms: ad timeouts, slot counts and ad load ship behind an experiment with contacts per session as the guardrail.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The last section of advertising-platforms performs the part's closing: it states what the five chapters build in common for every revenue line, says why that matters for Part VII, and returns to the part introduction's test of unit, liquidity spent and proof of delivery.

thesis.question: How do contacts become deals, and deals revenue, without selling out liquidity?
thesis.claim: Conversion and monetization in a listing marketplace should be built as one pipeline in which every revenue line has a record both sides can count and a guardrail on the match rate it spends: the contact is two objects: a platform-held conversation behind a synchronous safety gate and a lead with a stable ID that portal and professional count alike; the marketplace takes part in the transaction only in categories where items ship at moderate prices between strangers, letting a licensed provider hold the money while it owns the order, ledger and disputes; the unit of charge selects the system of record, and each model ships with a guardrail metric owned outside the team that books the revenue; catalog, price, an append-only entitlement ledger and the bill stay apart, with paid effects projected as explicit fields and every invoice line reconciled to delivery events; and display, sponsored listings and retail media run on three paths under one ad policy layer whose changes ship only with contacts per session as the guardrail; and a group shares this machinery beneath its brands while products, prices and the page stay with each brand.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of treating each revenue line as a product owned by its own team and optimized against its own revenue metric: chat built for delivery speed with checks after delivery or on reports, leads sent as e-mails, payments added as a checkout wherever product wants GMV, package checks written as conditions in the insertion service, the search query and a monthly billing export, and ad load and auction timeouts set by the ad team against eCPM.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this funds the shared conversation service and safety gate, the lead contract, the transaction platform and the entitlement ledger before new revenue models; requires every model, price event and ad change to name its unit, its system of truth, its delivery evidence and a liquidity guardrail with a stop condition before launch; puts all paid positions, whoever sells them, under one relevance floor and slot cap; and reports the lead reconciliation gap, unmatched clearing items and the daily unexplained billing difference next to contacts per session.
thesis.how_why: Veldmark's 2027 money incidents each came from a revenue line or contact path built without such a record or guardrail. A phishing link imitating Safe Deal reached Femke sixteen minutes after her first buyer contact because the check ran after delivery. The Essen Golf produced 23 leads for Motorvane and 14 in the dealer's CRM. About €2.3 million of Safe Deal items sat unmatched in clearing at the December 2026 month-end. Two counters billed 1,140 Motorvane dealers about €212,000 for cars that were never published. A longer header-bidding timeout raised programmatic revenue per page view about 4% while nobody measured contacts; the faster arm later chosen lost 1.9% of that revenue and gained about 1% in contacts.

supporting_claims.claim: A contact is two objects with different owners and retention: a conversation held by the platform, whose messages pass a synchronous safety gate with a fixed latency budget and four verdicts before the recipient sees them, and a lead governed as a versioned contract with the professional's systems (creation and deduplication rule, stable lead ID, acknowledged delivery, outcome feedback), so that portal and professional count the same leads before any lead is billed.

Taking part in the transaction is a per-category decision, made where the item ships, the price is moderate, the buyer fears non-delivery and the sale is otherwise between strangers, and held as configuration that can be switched off; a licensed provider's marketplace product holds the money while the marketplace owns six contexts (order, payment edge, fees, shipping, buyer protection and disputes, transaction ledger and tax reporting), with the ledger and dispute desk shipped with the checkout.

The unit of charge (listing, position, account, lead, transaction or audience) selects the system of record, and every model spends organic liquidity, so no model, price event or package change goes live without a named guardrail metric, a stop condition agreed in advance and an owner outside the team that books the revenue, with prices held as data and effects measured causally.

Catalog, price, entitlement and bill stay apart: entitlements are an append-only ledger with idempotency keys, enforcement points read effects projected as explicit paid fields on the listing read model, and delivery events from insertion, ranking, rendering, lead routing and ad serving are reconciled daily with grants and invoice lines.

Advertising is three businesses on three decision paths (ad server with header bidding, sponsored listings inside ranking, retail media through a consented audience service) under one ad policy layer owned by the product organization: timeout, slot-count and ad-load changes ship behind experiments with contacts per session as the guardrail, every paid position obeys one relevance floor and slot cap, and audiences exclude special-category data, minors and data held in a neutral role.

A group shares the money machinery beneath its brands (the conversation service and safety gate, the lead contract, the transaction platform among the profiles that use it, the catalog model and entitlement ledger, the ad stack and audience service) while products, prices, catalog content, contract terms, the choice of model and the page stay with each brand, and data the group holds in a neutral role stays out of lead outcomes, audiences and the shared ledger.

role.contribution: Follows the match into contact, deal and revenue, and names the guardrails and records that stop revenue from spending liquidity unseen.

additional_patterns.applies_to: messaging-and-leads to transactions-and-payments: money followed in the order it arises, from the contact to the deal
monetization-models to products-and-entitlements: from the choice of model to the commercial core that implements every model

flow.rationale: Each chapter prices or records something the one before it produced. Messaging comes first because the contact is the first thing the marketplace can count and charge for: it defines the lead that monetization prices and products-and-entitlements bills, and the offer in chat where transactions begin; placed after monetization, the per-lead proposal would be judged before the reader knows what a lead is or why 23 contacts are 19 leads. Transactions follow the contact into the deal and add the transactional revenue line; placed after monetization, the take rate would be one of ten models before the reader has seen the order, ledger and dispute systems it requires. Monetization then leaves the chronology: it surveys all ten models, including those charged at publication or in search before any contact, which it can judge only once the lead and the take rate have been shown with their systems, and ends on the missing piece all three Veldmark proposals hit, one record of what a seller bought and received; products-and-entitlements designs that record, and placed first it would build a catalog and ledger for models the reader has not met. Advertising comes last because it is the one line paid for attention rather than matches and it reuses the earlier chapters' machinery: sponsored listings join the product family and relevance floor that products-and-entitlements and ranking set, and its contacts guardrail measures the leads messaging defines; placed earlier, Decision 3 (one family of paid positions in the group catalog) would cite a catalog not yet designed. It also hands Part VII the platform demands (consent on every event, contacts as a governed metric).

hook.content: Part V made contact between strangers safe enough to happen. A classifieds site usually steps aside before the sale, so it charges for access to attention: the right to list, a better position, a package of slots, a lead, an advertisement.

opening.bridge: From Part V's trust platform, whose message gate, DAC7 perimeter and trader records Part VI inherits, to the conflict built into a marketplace's revenue: it earns its core revenue when buyers find the right listing quickly, while many revenue lines earn more when buyers see more pages or paid listings displace relevant ones.
opening.roadmap: Five chapters in the order money arises: messaging and leads, transactions and payments, monetization models, products and entitlements, advertising platforms; framed by Veldmark's €1.31 billion of 2026 revenue sold through four catalogs and a group ad unit, the Rotterdam city bike and the Essen Golf's 23 raw leads, and five 2027 decisions (one conversation service and lead contract, three monetization proposals, Veldmark Ads rules, the transaction platform funded first, Tally); ending on the test that for any paid product the reader can say which unit it charges for, what liquidity it spends and how they would prove it was delivered.

closing.synthesis: The five chapters give every revenue line the same three things: a record both sides can count (the lead ID, the order and transaction ledger, the entitlement ledger, one invoice line per paid position), delivery events that prove the record, and a guardrail that measures what the line costs the match rate. Money is one pipeline because those records and guardrails are shared, not because one team sells everything.
closing.so_what: Those records and guardrails are platform demands: leads and paid effects travel as events, contacts per session becomes a governed metric with one definition, price and ad changes need experiments with guardrails, and consent must reach every event; Part VII builds that platform, and a group without it re-creates the four-catalog problem in every brand.
closing.callback: The part introduction's closing test: for any paid product, which unit it charges for, what liquidity it spends, and how you would prove it was delivered.

takeaway.content: Review every revenue change as a change to the match rate, with its record, its delivery evidence and its guardrail named before launch; Part VII begins with event-driven-listings, the stream these records ride on.

transition_in.carries_over: Part V's threads, as marketplace-regulation hands them on: the message safety gate from the trust-and-safety platform, the DAC7 perimeter that in-platform payments cross, labels that govern paid placements, and trader records that feed billing.
transition_in.introduces: The next step after a safe contact: the conversation and lead, the deal, and the revenue lines built on them.

thesis.question: How should a marketplace connect buyers and sellers so contacts become deals, without creating a scam channel?

thesis.question: When and how should a classifieds marketplace move into transactions, and what does it take architecturally?
thesis.claim: A classifieds marketplace should take part in the transaction per category, not per brand, and only where the item ships, the price is moderate (tens to a few hundred euros), the buyer's main fear is non-delivery and the sale is otherwise between strangers, gated as configuration per country and category so it can be switched off; a licensed provider's marketplace product should hold the money and verify payees, while the marketplace owns six contexts beside the listing core (order with availability and timers, payment edge, fees, shipping, buyer protection and disputes, and the transaction ledger with tax reporting), and the ledger, release rules and dispute desk ship with the checkout rather than after it.
thesis.disputed_by: Two opposite views: that a classifieds marketplace should stay out of payments entirely to remain cheap to run and free of payment regulation, or that it should make every brand and category transactional to capture a take rate, launching the checkout as a product feature and adding the ledger and dispute handling once volume justifies them.

thesis.question: Which revenue models fit which marketplace, and what does each require from the systems?
thesis.claim: A revenue model fits a marketplace only where its unit of charge matches how that marketplace's sellers sell and where the marketplace can count and prove delivery of that unit: paid visibility where free private supply is large, slot subscriptions where professionals list continuously, per-lead fees only where leads are deduplicated across channels and reconcilable with the professional's CRM, take rates where goods ship and protection is worth paying for, and pay at close only where outcomes are observable; the unit (listing, position, account, lead, transaction or audience) selects the system of record, and the KPI a portal publishes (ARPA, ARPR, yield per listing, take rate) reveals which unit it chose; and because every model spends organic liquidity (insertion fees spend supply depth, paid positions relevance, lead fees professional trust, advertising page speed and attention), none should go live without a named guardrail metric, a stop condition agreed in advance and an owner outside the team that books the revenue.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that choosing a revenue model is a pricing and commercial decision for the monetization team, judged by its business case and revenue forecast, with the systems adapted afterwards and liquidity effects left to show up in next year's numbers.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this puts four questions to every revenue proposal (what unit, which system holds the truth about what was sold, what it costs in liquidity, who notices first), requires a model readiness card (unit, system of truth, delivery evidence, dispute process, accounting treatment, regulatory review, rollback) before launch, has the group own one catalog model, entitlement service and metering standard so a new model is configuration rather than a fifth implementation, holds prices and packages as data that can be rolled back, and funds experiments or matched comparisons to measure package ROI.

thesis.question: How do you architect what a seller can buy, what they are entitled to, and how they are billed?
thesis.claim: The commercial core behind paid products should keep four concerns apart, a versioned product catalog, a pricing engine, an entitlement ledger and billing, so that a price event is a reviewed data release rather than a code release; entitlements should be an append-only ledger of grants, consumptions, releases, expiries and refunds with idempotency keys rather than counters in each service; enforcement points should read effects projected through events as explicit paid fields on the listing read model, never asking the ledger live and never letting an effect outlive the listing's sale or removal; and insertion, ranking, rendering and lead routing should emit delivery events that a daily reconciliation compares with grants and invoice lines, so that every invoice line traces to delivery.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of writing package checks as conditions in the insertion service, the search query and the card template, with a monthly billing export counting by its own definition; or a counter service per quota; or a billing vendor's feature switches taken as the entitlement system.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this makes the catalog model, the entitlement ledger, the effect schema and the delivery-evidence events group standards while leaving products, prices and contract terms to brands, writes an entitlement matrix naming each product's enforcement point, effect, evidence and owner, buys invoicing, tax and collection but builds the catalog, ledger and effect projector, moves each brand only after a shadow billing month reconciles with no unexplained difference, and watches the daily unexplained difference in euros.
thesis.how_why: Motorvane counted a dealer's cars twice: the feed importer published 150 of Autohaus Ruhrblick's 163 cars and skipped 13, while the billing export counted the feed file and charged €117 overage for cars never live; an audit found 1,140 dealers overbilled by about €212,000 over 14 months. The same missing record made the 1 January 2028 price event an estimate in engineering weeks per brand. At Veldmark's Sunday peak of 31,000 queries a second, a ranking stage asking the ledger live for 400 candidates per query (an illustrative figure) would need on the order of 12 million answers a second, so effects must ride on the listing document. Under Tally, Ruhrblick's month records 150 consumptions and 13 refused publications, and the invoice carries no overage line.

role.contribution: Designs the commercial core that implements every monetization model and supplies the part's proof that what was sold was delivered, with paid effects that ranking and advertising consume.

posts.title: Selling Attention: Display, Native and Retail-Media Advertising
posts.question: How do marketplaces run advertising alongside listings without degrading the experience or breaking privacy law?

know: Advertising as three businesses (display and native, sponsored listings, retail media), the components of a marketplace ad stack and who owns each.
The header-bidding timeout trade-off and page-speed rules for ad slots; why sponsored listings belong inside ranking and the regulatory floor for paid ranking (Omnibus, P2B, DSA Art. 26).
Consent architecture (TCF, certified CMPs, the EDPB consent-or-pay opinion) and a first-party audience service with consent checks, exclusions, minimum sizes and controlled activation.
believe: Consent and latency set the ceiling on display revenue, so changes to them are revenue changes and match-rate changes that need experiments and guardrails.
First-party intent data is the marketplace's advantage and its main liability, and data held in a neutral role stays out of advertising.
can_do: Set an ad-change rule with contacts per session as the guardrail and run the experiment that tests it.
Design an audience service whose segments are consented, purpose-bound and approved by the data-protection officer.
Put every paid position, whoever sells it, under one relevance floor and slot cap and one invoice line.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given three advertising conflicts, the reader names the component that decides each and the rule it applies.

Using only this chapter: what decides each, and what rule applies?

Audiences come from the first-party audience service, built only from consented, purpose-bound sources approved by the data-protection officer, excluding dealer-side, neutral-role and message data, with a minimum size and off-site activation through a clean room. Both paid products become one product family in the group catalog, decided inside ranking under one relevance floor and slot cap (at most three paid positions in the first ten rows), shown on one invoice line.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Advertising as the part's last revenue line and the only one paid for attention rather than matches; the tension between core revenue and page views; the three businesses and the terms the chapter owns; then Veldmark Ads and its three arguments, vocabulary, three stacks under one policy layer, consent, the public record, three 2027 decisions, trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: investor sources (Adevinta, eBay, CarGurus, Autotrader, Rightmove), EU law and the EDPB, IAB and Prebid documentation, and the fictional Veldmark.

thesis.question: How do marketplaces run advertising alongside listings without degrading the experience or breaking privacy law?
thesis.claim: Advertising on a listing marketplace is three businesses that should run on three decision paths, display and native through an ad server with header bidding, sponsored listings inside each brand's search and ranking, and retail media through a consented first-party audience service, under one ad policy service, held as configuration by the product organization that owns the page, which sets ad load, labels, exclusions and the floors and caps on paid positions; changes to auction timeouts, slot counts or ad load ship only behind an experiment with contacts per session as the guardrail; fixed-price and auctioned paid positions share one relevance floor and slot cap; and audiences are built only from consented, purpose-bound sources, excluding special-category data, minors and data the group holds in a neutral role.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that advertising is a separate business unit optimized against eCPM, fill rate and revenue per page view, which sets its own timeouts, ad load and sponsored placements on result pages and builds audiences from whatever behavioral data the group holds.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this shares the ad server, header bidding, consent integration, audience service and measurement as one group stack but serves sponsored listings inside each brand's ranking, puts all paid positions in one product family in the group catalog, has the data-protection officer approve every audience purpose with exclusions enforced by access control, keeps the campaign, targeting and reporting model group-owned to limit vendor dependency, and shows eCPM and fill rate next to contacts per session and page speed on one dashboard.
thesis.how_why: Veldmark Ads earned €100 million in 2026. Raising the Prebid timeout on Tradeyard Netherlands from 1,000 to 1,500 ms lifted programmatic revenue per thousand page views about 4% but worsened the 75th-percentile largest contentful paint from 2.4 to 2.9 seconds on a site where 46% of sessions start from organic search, and nobody measured contacts; in the July 2027 experiment, 900 ms with server-side bidders and lazy loading lost 1.9% of that revenue and gained about 1% in contacts, which is worth more because contacts drive renewals, VAS purchases and Safe Deal transactions. A car maker's 'electric SUV' segment fell from about 310,000 to about 240,000 users once consent purposes were checked. On Tradeyard Poland a seller could pay twice, on two invoices, for a Top listing and a Sponsored campaign claiming the same rows, the second outside the relevance floor.

role.contribution: Adds the one revenue line paid for attention rather than matches, puts it under the same guardrails and product family as the others, and carries the part's closing into Part VII's platform demands.

transition_in.introduces: Advertising, which sells the audience rather than the listing, to brands and agencies rather than sellers, through ad servers, header bidding and consent signals.

parts.title: Part VII — PLATFORM: The Distributed System Underneath

know: The listing event as a published contract: one emitting owner, transactional outbox or change data capture behind a translator, per-listing keys and versions, state-carrying events, schema compatibility rules, replay, dead letters and a removal objective tighter than the publication objective.

One system of record per listing fact and the consumer registry of copies, each with owner, staleness budget per read path, rebuild path and retention per data class; erasure as a workflow with receipts and an erasure ledger.

The customer-facing layer: landing pages generated from demand and supply rules, URLs, status codes and sitemaps driven by lifecycle events, server rendering with page-level ownership, backends-for-frontends, and answer engines as a channel.

The data platform's three contracts (tracking plan, governed liquidity metrics starting with a qualified contact, purpose-bound access) on one tenant-partitioned lakehouse with domain-owned data products.

Experimentation in a two-sided market: the four platform contracts, interference, randomization units (listing, two-sided, cluster, switchback) and marketplace guardrails; ML governance by decision tier (inform, order, gate, commit) on a shared path of features, labels and prediction logs.

The tenancy model (tenant code everywhere, configuration hierarchy, extension points, forks with expiry, release rings, group-urgent changes, exit paths), journey objectives with error budgets, the degradation ladder, and cost per thousand searches, per live listing and per contact.
believe: A shared platform is trusted because its contracts hold and are checked, not because brands are told to use it.
Every copy, metric, experiment and model needs a registered owner and a written promise, or it becomes a place where stale, wrong or unlawful data is served.
Sharing belongs beneath the product, decided capability by capability, so a group can reverse a sharing decision without rewriting its brands.
can_do: For any listing fact, say where it is true, which copies hold it, how stale each may be, and how each would be rebuilt or erased.
Review a platform proposal (an event schema, a new copy, a metric, a test design, a model use, a fork, an objective) by its owner, its contract and the check that proves the contract holds.
Decide which platform capabilities a group shares first and which stay with each brand, and what each tenant needs to be able to leave.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
A reader who has read only Part VII can assign six platform incidents to the chapter whose design owns each and name the control that design applies.
acceptance_criteria.probe: In one year at a marketplace group: a morning alert e-mail still features a bike that sold the previous evening; a seller's erasure request takes two days just to find where her listing is stored, and two of the copies are public; each brand reports a different number of contacts for the same week; a price cut for a paid bump wins a seller-randomized test with +18% revenue and loses money after rollout; a fraud rule written in one country reaches the second three days later and never reaches two others; and search fails for 48 minutes on a Sunday evening when a TV campaign meets a scheduled reindex. Using only Part VII, which chapter's design owns each, and what does it do?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Event-driven listings: the digest consumes ListingSold from the one owned stream and re-checks state at send time. Listing data management: a consumer registry of copies with owners, and an erasure workflow in which every copy returns a receipt to a ledger. Data platform: one governed definition of a qualified contact with a steward and a version, computed once. Experimentation: interference; randomize by cluster or listing for a visibility product, with a control-trend guardrail. Multi-country platforms: the tenant as a first-class element, fraud rules as a group-urgent change class reaching every tenant at once. Reliability and scale: journey objectives with error budgets, a peak calendar that blocks batch work, and a degradation ladder that sheds bots and optional features first.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The last section of reliability-and-scale performs the part's closing: it states what the eight chapters build in common, says why that matters for Part VIII, and returns to the part introduction's test of where a listing fact is true and how its copies are rebuilt or erased.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Does the final section of reliability-and-scale state something about Part VII that no single chapter states, say why it matters for Part VIII, and return to the question the part introduction ends on?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A synthesis that each platform capability is a published contract with an owner, a registry and a check (event contract, consumer registry, lifecycle rules, governed metrics, experiment standard, model registry, tenancy model, journey objectives); a so-what that building those contracts across acquired brands and old teams is a problem of change and ownership, which Part VIII takes up; an explicit return to the introduction's test (for any listing fact, where it is true, which copies hold it and how you would rebuild or erase them).

thesis.question: What must the platform beneath a group's marketplaces guarantee, and in what form should it be shared, so that every stage above it can rely on it?
thesis.claim: The platform beneath a group's marketplaces should be a set of published contracts, each with an owner and a check, that brands adopt because the contracts hold rather than because they are mandated: one owned, versioned and replayable listing event stream from which every copy is built; a register of every copy with its staleness budget, rebuild path and retention, through which removals and erasures reach each copy with a receipt; URLs, status codes and sitemaps driven by the same lifecycle events; a tracking plan and a short catalog of governed liquidity metrics, starting with one definition of a contact; experiments randomized by the mechanism a change works through, with guardrails for the side not tested; models governed by the decision they make; the tenant as a first-class element, with market differences held as configuration and forks allowed only with an expiry date; and reliability set as journey objectives with error budgets and unit costs. Shared this way, beneath the brands, the platform lets each marketplace change its product without breaking the others.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice in which the platform grows from private integrations (polling jobs, replica reads, nightly dumps, copied country codebases) and each brand keeps its own warehouse, metric definitions, experiment tool and model stack; or the opposite response, a central platform team that mandates one product stack for every brand and measures itself by service uptime and run-cost savings.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this funds the listing event contract, the consumer registry and the governed contact metric before any shared product surface; makes registration a condition of access for every consumer, copy and production model; requires an expiry date on every brand fork and an exit path for every tenant of a shared capability; and reports journey error budgets, cost per thousand searches and contacts from organic sessions in place of indexed URLs, service uptime or model counts.
thesis.how_why: Veldmark's 2027 platform incidents each came from a missing contract. Tradeyard NL had eleven readers of listing changes on five mechanisms and nobody had the list, so a digest featured Femke's bike the morning after it sold; six months later her erasure request found seven copies, two of them public. Tradeyard's dashboard counted 52 contacts for the bike where one governed definition counts 13. A seller-randomized bump test forecast +18% revenue and lost about 2.5% after rollout, because treated sellers took first-page time from control sellers. Of 146 production models, 23 had no owner. A phishing rule reached Belgium three days late and Poland and Portugal never. A TV campaign and a scheduled reindex browned out search for 48 minutes and cost about 9,800 first contacts.

supporting_claims.claim: Listing changes reach every downstream reader through one owned, versioned stream that only the listing's system of record emits, published in the same transaction as the change, keyed and versioned per listing so consumers apply each change once and in order, carrying current public state so a lost message heals, evolved under explicit compatibility rules, replayable, and held to a removal objective tighter than the publication objective.

Each listing fact has one system of record, and every other store is a copy registered before it gets access, with an owner, a staleness budget per read path, a rebuild path and a retention rule per data class, so corrections, removals and erasures reach every copy and each copy owner returns a receipt.

The public web is a copy with external readers: landing pages generated from demand and live supply under explicit rules are the durable search inventory, canonical URLs, status codes and sitemaps follow the listing lifecycle events, pages are server-rendered with one owning team per URL pattern and apps get their own backends, and the layer is judged by contacts from organic sessions, not by indexed URLs.

A tracking plan with server-side facts, a short catalog of governed liquidity metrics, each with one steward, definition, computation and version, and purpose-bound access policy are the contracts of the data platform, with domains owning data products on one shared, tenant-partitioned substrate.

Because buyers and sellers affect each other, experiments are built on agreeing assignment, exposure, metric and analysis contracts, randomized by the mechanism a change works through rather than by user by default, guarded on the side not tested, and pre-registered and reviewed when they change visibility, prices, fees or trust thresholds.

Every production model is registered with an owner, a decision tier per consumer (inform, order, gate, commit), a label definition, a monitor and a cost; the tier, not the algorithm, sets the validation and approval, and a model moves up a tier only with a new validation regime and a limit on the money it can commit.

A group shares a platform beneath its brands by making the tenant a first-class element of every shared capability, holding market differences as versioned configuration and owned extension points, allowing forks only with an expiry date, releasing in rings with group-urgent changes reaching all tenants at once, giving every tenant an exit path, holding each platform team accountable to its tenants for service levels and cost and measuring its adoption without mandate, and sharing first the capabilities whose technology is uniform and whose value grows with pooled data.

Reliability is set per liquidity journey as objectives with error budgets that restrict change, peaks are planned with a calendar that keeps batch work out of them and a degradation ladder that gives up bots and optional features before search, and cost per thousand searches, per live listing and per contact is reported per owner.

role.contribution: Builds the platform the six stages stand on as a set of published contracts, so a group can share it beneath its brands without coupling brands to each other's internals.

additional_patterns.applies_to: event-driven-listings to web-and-seo-architecture: one listing change followed outward, from the system of record onto the stream, into the internal copies, and onto the public web and the search engines' copy of it

flow.rationale: Each chapter builds on a contract an earlier one published. The event stream comes first because every later chapter reads it: copies are rebuilt from it, sitemaps and status codes follow its lifecycle events, the listing-history data product and event-triggered model scoring consume it, and its envelope is the first place the tenant code is carried; placed later, each of those chapters would have to describe its own feed. Listing data management follows because the stream is what makes copies cheap, and the consumer registry extends the stream's consumer list to every store; placed before the stream, staleness budgets would have nothing to be measured against. Web and SEO follows as the copy with external readers and the first chapter to judge a layer by a liquidity metric (contacts from organic sessions), which raises the question the data platform answers: one governed definition of a contact. Experimentation needs the data platform's governed metrics and exposure context to measure causation; placed before it, the bump post-mortem's fix (governed primary metrics and guardrails) would cite metrics not yet defined. The ML platform needs both: features and labels from the data platform, and experiments randomized by district to test the pricing badge; placed before them, its order-tier gate (online experiments with two-sided metrics) and its label contracts would cite a standard and metrics the reader has not met. Multi-country platforms comes after the capabilities because it decides how each of them is shared across tenants, and it scores the capabilities the reader has now met; placed first, the tenancy model would govern capabilities not yet designed. Reliability and scale comes last because its journeys cross the whole platform (the listing-gone journey runs on the stream, cost per search spans engines the tenancy decisions consolidate) and because it hands to Part VIII the problem of building all this across acquired brands; placed earlier, the listing-gone journey would measure a removal path not yet built, and unit costs and the shared search platform would assume tenancy decisions not yet made.

hook.content: Parts II to VI designed what a marketplace does. Most groups never designed the layer all of that stands on: it grew from polling jobs, nightly dumps and copied country codebases.

opening.bridge: From Part VI's revenue lines, which assumed events for paid effects and leads, contacts as a governed metric and experiments for price and ad changes, to the distributed system beneath every stage, and to Veldmark starting 2027 with four messaging technologies, three warehouses, 146 production models on four training stacks and a monolith full of country branches.
opening.roadmap: Eight chapters: event-driven listings, listing data management, web and SEO architecture, the data platform, experimentation, the ML platform, multi-country platforms, reliability and scale; framed by the 48-minute Sunday-evening brown-out and Veldmark's 2027 decisions (journey objectives, server-rendered pages and event-driven sitemaps, Tenancy model v1, Experimentation standard v1, Listing event contract v1, the Iceberg data platform, the retention schedule and extended consumer registry, the group model registry); ending on the test that for any listing fact the reader can say where it is true, which copies hold it and how they would rebuild or erase them.

closing.synthesis: The eight chapters give each platform capability the same three things: a published contract (the listing event, the copy register entry, the lifecycle rule, the metric definition, the experiment standard, the model registry entry, the tenant code and configuration schema, the journey objective), an owner, and a check that shows whether the contract holds. That is what lets brands rely on the platform without being ordered to.
closing.so_what: The contracts exist on paper before they exist in a group assembled by acquisition: four brands must move onto them, teams must be organized to own them, and the monolith must be retired while it serves traffic. That is a problem of change, which Part VIII takes up.
closing.callback: The part introduction's closing test: for any listing fact, where it is true, which copies hold it, and how you would rebuild or erase them.

takeaway.content: Ask of every platform capability who owns its contract and what check proves it holds; Part VIII begins with platform-consolidation, the order in which acquired stacks move onto these contracts.

transition_in.carries_over: Advertising-platforms' closing: the ad stack needed a consent signal on every event, a read model of paid positions inside ranking and measurement that joins impressions to contacts, and Part VI as a whole assumed events for leads and paid effects, contact counts and pricing tests without building them.
transition_in.introduces: The distributed system beneath every stage: events, copies, the public web, data, experimentation, ML, tenancy and reliability.

posts.title: Every Change Is an Event: Event-Driven Listing Architecture
posts.question: How should listing changes flow to search, trust, alerts, analytics and partners?

know: The difference between domain events, change events and commands; notification, event-carried state transfer and event sourcing; ordering, delivery guarantees and idempotency.

The listing event stream: components, the transactional outbox, change data capture behind a translator during migration, the event envelope (listing key, aggregate version, cause, public state), the event catalog, topics and retention.

Schema evolution under compatibility modes and the rules Veldmark publishes; replay, backfills and dead letters that cannot resurrect a sold listing; removal objectives separate from publication objectives.
believe: The listing event is a published contract with one owner, not an integration detail, and change data capture is a source, not a contract.
Reliable publication and safe consumption are two halves, and neither alone gives correct downstream state.
can_do: Review a listing event design and say what goes wrong at the weekly peak, during a backfill or after a schema change.
Design an envelope, a version-gated consumer and a replay path that keeps sold listings removed.
Decide which parts of the event contract a group sets centrally and which each brand keeps.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a stale downstream copy and a replay plan, the reader names the mechanism that fixes each.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A listing sells at 18:10 and leaves search at 18:11, but the next morning's alert digest, built the afternoon before from a database replica, still features it. Separately, a team plans to rebuild the search index by replaying six months of listing events and fears that old events will bring sold listings back. Using only this chapter: what design fixes the digest, and what makes the replay safe?
acceptance_criteria.expected: One owned listing event stream emitted by the system of record through an outbox (or CDC behind a translator), to which the digest subscribes, so ListingSold removes the bike; and a derived artifact that re-checks listing state at send time. Consumers apply events only when the per-listing version is higher than the one they hold, events carry current public state, and the replay reads a compacted state topic where sold listings end in tombstones, so no old event resurrects a sold listing.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A listing written once and read by ten or twenty systems, so the question is how changes move, not how they are stored; one published stream replacing private integrations; the chapter opening Part VII and owning the listing event, outbox and schema evolution, with copies and tracking left to the next chapters. Then the bike incident at Veldmark, event concepts, the stream's architecture, public evidence and Listing event contract v1, schema evolution, replay and dead letters, trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: dated classifieds engineering sources (Adevinta, Kleinanzeigen, Vinted, AutoScout24, mobile.de), Confluent and Debezium documentation, and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How should listing changes flow to search, trust, alerts, analytics and partners?
thesis.claim: Listing changes should reach search, alerts, trust and safety, SEO, analytics and partners through one owned, versioned stream of listing events that only the listing's system of record emits: published in the same transaction as the change (a transactional outbox, or change data capture behind a translator while a monolith remains), keyed by listing ID with a strictly increasing per-listing version that consumers use to apply each change once and in order, carrying the listing's current public state so a consumer recovers from a lost message with the next one, evolved under full transitive schema compatibility with semantic changes reviewed by people, replayable from a compacted state topic, and held to a removal objective tighter than the publication objective (at Veldmark p99 under five seconds to topic and under thirty seconds to search deletion).
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of letting each downstream system poll the listing database or a replica, receive nightly dumps or messages the application sends after commit, or read change-data-capture rows as its contract, with each producing team choosing its own event names and payloads.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this decides centrally the envelope, the cross-brand listing identity, the event catalog, the compatibility rules, the removal service levels and per-topic access, and leaves each brand its internal events and its choice of outbox or CDC during migration; makes consumers register before they get access; and watches publication and end-to-end removal latency per tenant, consumer lag at the Sunday-evening peak and the count of consumers still reading producer tables.
thesis.how_why: Femke's bike sold at 18:10 and left Solr at 18:11, but the next morning's digest, assembled from a MySQL replica the afternoon before, still featured it, and three people messaged her. Tradeyard NL alone had eleven readers of listing changes on five mechanisms, and nobody had the list. Replayed on Listing event contract v1, the ListingSold event at version 9 reaches the digest, which also re-checks state at send time. The contract went live on 1 July 2027 with 23 consumer groups and by the end of 2027 carried about 4.2 million events a day; content-hash suppression keeps about a million no-op updates a day off the stream. The Essen Golf's removal, reported by the dealer's feed 26 hours late, shows the limit: the stream makes copies as fresh as the source, not fresher.

role.contribution: Publishes the first platform contract, the listing event stream, that every later chapter of the part reads from.
