acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Who owns which journey, capability and decision; team types and interaction modes; platform teams as internal products; decision rights, the advice process and funding; the terms marketplace team topology and architecture governance; evidence from documented reorganizations of classifieds groups and the fictional Veldmark's Common Ground organization and advice forum.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: Which organizational design makes a multi-marketplace architecture work?
thesis.claim: A group of marketplaces builds each shared capability once and gets a fix, such as a fraud rule, into every brand and country within hours rather than days only when every buyer and seller journey, bounded context and shared capability has exactly one owning team within its cognitive load: stream-aligned brand teams cut by journey rather than by country, platform teams that offer shared capabilities as internal products with a published contract, a roadmap and migration help, and specialist teams only for rare subsystems such as ranking and valuation; and when cross-brand decisions are made through an open, recorded advice process under an explicit matrix of what the group, the platforms and each brand decide, rather than by an architecture review board that owns nothing.
thesis.disputed_by: Federated guilds in which brand teams build platforms 'on behalf of the group' and nobody owns them; or a central product-and-technology organization that owns every product and platform, adopted by mandate and deadline and governed by an architecture review board that approves designs.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this reviews the capability map, the context map and the team topology together twice a year and treats any orphaned or split ownership as a defect with a fix and a date; measures each platform team by tenants in production, onboarding cost and remaining shadow copies; funds platform build centrally, then by showback, then by allocation, fixed for policy-driven platforms such as trust and safety; and keeps escalations from the advice forum to about one decision in ten.
thesis.how_why: On 7 March 2027 a phishing rule written by Tradeyard Netherlands reached Belgium on 10 March, with a Yardstick deploy, and never reached Poland or Portugal, whose moderation two outsourced vendors ran; Motorvane never learned that the fraudster's phone number had registered there. Veldmark had about 1,150 engineers in 158 teams, and none of the nine Common Ground capabilities had exactly one owning team. After Common Ground organization v1 (decided 22 June 2027), by December 8 of 9 did, country-cut teams fell from 17 to 4, and cognitive-load flags from 23 to 9; the forum logged 74 cross-brand decisions at a median of nine working days, six escalated to the CTO. Replayed on the shared platform, the rule reached every subscribing tenant within an hour: the rule engine had not changed, the ownership had.

role.contribution: Assigns an owning team to every journey, context and shared capability that consolidation moves, and sets the decision rights and forum through which cross-brand decisions are made.

transition_in.carries_over: Platform-consolidation's closing: a consolidation sequence says what moves and when, but not who owns each capability once it has moved or how the acquired engineers become part of the group.
transition_in.introduces: The marketplace team topology and architecture governance: one owning team per journey, context and capability, platform teams as internal products, decision rights, the advice process and funding.

posts.title: Changing the Engine in Flight: Modernizing a Live Marketplace
posts.question: How do you move a live marketplace from legacy systems to a new architecture without losing traffic, sellers or revenue?

know: Re-architect, re-platform and rewrite; seams and transitional architecture (edge routes, backends-for-frontends, event interception, branch by abstraction); parallel run, shadow traffic and canary; the migration stage gate.

Data migration of listings and accounts with one writer per record, search migration with relevance parity, URL migration, the behavior catalog, kill switches, rollback and points of no return, and how to measure progress.
believe: A live marketplace is migrated by slices behind seams, never by a rewrite and a single cut-over.
Parity means equal outcomes for buyers and sellers, not equal features or identical results.
can_do: Order a monolith's capabilities into migration waves and name the seam for each.
Write stage gates with numerical exit criteria and a rollback answer for a slice, including relevance parity for a search move.
Decide in advance where a migration's points of no return are.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a migration proposal that relies on a rewrite and identical results, the reader names the plan, gates and parity measure that replace it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A classifieds site's twenty-year-old monolith holds the listing table, renders most pages, runs undocumented scheduled jobs and serves old app versions directly. The proposal is to build the new platform to feature parity and switch over on one weekend, and to accept the new search engine when its top-ten results match the old engine's for 95% of head queries. Using only this chapter: what do you propose instead?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Put seams in front of the monolith (edge routes, backends-for-frontends, event interception) and move slices: read paths first, the write path that unblocks most teams next, search after it, the system of record's archive last; give each slice an owning team and a behavior catalog that decides what to carry, change or retire; pass each slice through contract, shadow, canary, ramp and retire gates with numbers agreed in advance and rehearsed rollback; judge search by relevance parity (non-inferior contacts per search session in an experiment, with latency and zero-result checks), not identical results; build the new index from the event stream, not from the old index; keep URLs stable unless a change is decided; record points of no return as decisions.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Retiring a monolith while it serves traffic: slices and their order, seams, parallel runs, data migration, search migration with relevance parity, URL stability and when rollback stops being possible; the terms migration stage gate, relevance parity and URL migration; evidence from the strangler-fig literature and documented classifieds migrations, and the fictional Veldmark's plan to retire Yardstick by the end of 2029.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How do you move a live marketplace from legacy systems to a new architecture without losing traffic, sellers or revenue?
thesis.claim: A live marketplace should be moved off its monolith slice by slice behind seams that can route traffic back in minutes (edge routes, backends-for-frontends, the event stream): read paths first, then the write path that unblocks the most teams, then search, with the system of record's archive last. Each slice should be owned by a team of the target organization, should carry a catalog of legacy behaviors deliberately kept, changed or retired, and should pass stage gates (contract, shadow, canary, ramp, retire) whose numerical exit criteria are liquidity outcomes agreed before the slice starts, such as relevance parity measured as non-inferior contacts per search session rather than identical results; URLs should stay stable unless a change is decided, and every point of no return should be recorded as a decision before it is reached.
thesis.disputed_by: The rewrite: build the new platform beside the monolith to feature parity and switch over in one cut-over, judge the new search engine by how closely its results match the old one's, and treat rollback as an emergency procedure rather than a designed path.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this spends early on seams that deliver little visible value alone, has the advice forum review each slice's gate criteria before it starts, puts liquidity metrics (contacts, publication outcomes, billing, organic traffic) into every gate, reports the double-running cost and its end date, requires rollback rehearsals with real cohorts, and takes each point of no return as a recorded forum decision.
thesis.how_why: Yardstick, Tradeyard's PHP monolith, implemented 23 capabilities, had a 214-column listing table read by 38 modules, 47 scheduled jobs (9 without a known owner), 312 admin actions and 118 app endpoints, and its colocation contract ends on 31 December 2029. The Yardstick Exit plan moves it in waves 0 to 6. In the insertion shadow 6.8% of submissions first differed, and nine behaviors surfaced that the 146-item catalog had missed, among them a job that turned a price of €0 into 'price on request'. On Tradeyard Portugal, fewer than three-quarters of the new engine's top ten results matched the old engine's (median overlap 0.71), yet 8.8% of search sessions led to a contact against 8.7% on Solr, and the relevance parity gate passed. No listing URL changed in 2028, and capabilities implemented only in Yardstick fell from 23 to 6 by December 2028.

role.contribution: Supplies the techniques for moving a live marketplace onto the platforms and owners the previous chapters chose, slice by slice and gate by gate.

transition_in.carries_over: Organizing-marketplace-engineering's closing: the organization assigns owners but does not move code; Tradeyard's teams still deploy through Yardstick, and the new platform teams own capabilities the monolith still implements.
transition_in.introduces: Moving the code itself: seams, slices and waves, stage gates, relevance parity, URL migration and points of no return, through the Yardstick Exit plan.

posts.title: AI Across the Listing Lifecycle
posts.question: Where do AI and agents create value in listing marketplaces, and what architecture keeps them controlled?

know: Where generative AI and agents have shipped at marketplaces from 2023 to 2026 across the listing lifecycle (creation, search, moderation, pro tooling, valuation), and the autonomy ladder.

The control layer between models and listings (constrained generation, validation, provenance, trust checks before generation, the AI gateway and evaluation harness), conversational search as a query compiler, search as an API product for external agents, AI crawlers and data licensing, cost per outcome, evaluation, and the EU AI Act's dated obligations.
believe: A model's output is a proposal to be validated, never listing data.
The structured assets (taxonomy, attribute dictionary, search schema, trust rules) become more valuable when AI arrives, not less.
can_do: Review an AI proposal by asking what structured thing the model produces and what checks it.
Design an assisted insertion flow in which the platform validates every suggestion and records its provenance.
Register an AI use with its autonomy level, owner, evaluation set, cost per outcome, AI Act classification and kill switch.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an AI feature design that writes model output straight into listings, the reader names the controls the architecture lacks.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A marketplace launches an assistant that reads a seller's photos and writes the category, attributes, price and description straight into the listing, with the model choosing free-text values. Two weeks later its color filter has over a thousand distinct values, some prices are wrong, and fraud analysts say scam listings now read as well as genuine ones. Using only this chapter: what does the architecture lack, and what do you build?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A control layer in which the model proposes and the platform decides: screen photos against known scam images before generating; constrain the category to the taxonomy's current leaves and attribute values to the dictionary, returning 'unknown' rather than guessing; take the price range from a registered predictive model, never from the language model; draft text last with guardrails; require seller confirmation and record per-field provenance; shift fraud detection toward account, device, image and price signals; and register the use with an owner, evaluation set, cost per outcome and kill switch.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: AI as the translator between people and the marketplace's structures; where it has shipped across the listing lifecycle; the control layer that treats output as a proposal; the photo-to-listing assistant; search, external agents and crawlers; trust and safety, pro copilots and valuation; cost, evaluation and the EU AI Act; evidence from documented 2023–2026 marketplace launches, regulation and the fictional Veldmark's pilot.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: Where do AI and agents create value in listing marketplaces, and what architecture keeps them controlled?
thesis.claim: AI creates value in listing marketplaces where it translates people's intent into structures the marketplace already has (photos into a category and attributes, a sentence into search filters, a message into a policy label, a lead into a drafted reply). It stays controlled only behind a layer that treats every model output as a proposal: constrained to the taxonomy, the attribute dictionary and the search filter schema, validated and stored with per-field provenance, preceded by trust checks, and never the source of a number a buyer relies on, which comes from a registered predictive model. Search offered to external assistants becomes an API product with contracts, quotas and lead attribution, and every AI use is registered with its autonomy level, owner, evaluation set, cost per outcome, AI Act classification and kill switch.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that generative models make structured listing data less necessary, so a model can write free-text listings and answer buyers directly; or the practice of letting each team launch AI features from vendor demos, judged by uptake, with governance added after launch.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this extends the model registry into an AI use register and blocks launches that cannot fill it in; treats the taxonomy, attribute service, search API and trust platform as the AI strategy; runs one AI gateway and evaluation harness for the group while brand teams build the features; puts each brand's channel strategy toward external assistants in a decision record with a review date; enforces data-use rules in pipelines; and approves AI features by cost per outcome.
thesis.how_why: Veldmark's photo-to-listing pilot (approved 15 November 2027, 5% of Tradeyard Netherlands' private sellers, goods only) was possible only because the group taxonomy and attribute service went live in October and the shared trust-and-safety platform in November. In nine weeks it produced about 154,000 assisted listings: 62% uptake, 92.4% of categories accepted unchanged, 78% of attribute suggestions accepted, unsupported claims in 1.9% of audited descriptions, median insertion time 2 min 50 s against 6 min 40 s, and 9 percentage points more started listings published, at €0.0062 of model cost per listing. Constrained values raised the share of cargo-bike listings recording electric assist from 61% to 88%; an earlier prototype with free-text attributes produced 1,100 distinct colors in two weeks. Fraudsters used the assistant as often as anyone, removing poor text as a scam signal. The search platform's head asked who pays for an external assistant's queries at the Sunday-evening peak of 31,000 queries per second, which is why search offered to assistants needs contracts and quotas.

role.contribution: Extends model governance to generative AI and agents: AI proposes, the structured systems the earlier parts built decide, and every AI use is registered and costed.

transition_in.carries_over: Modernization-and-migration's closing: the platform that replaces Yardstick is delivered capability by capability, and its structured services (the taxonomy and attribute service, Listing Search API v1, the shared trust-and-safety platform) are what the next technology shift will run on.
transition_in.introduces: Generative AI and agents across the listing lifecycle, and the control layer that makes those structured services the system of record for every model proposal.

posts.title: Built to Be Replaced: Evolving a Marketplace Platform Over a Decade
posts.question: How does a Chief Architect keep a marketplace platform coherent over ten years of acquisitions, verticals, regulations and technology shifts?

know: The book's argument restated part by part: each part as a stage of the liquidity machine, the guarantee it must give, the liquidity metric it protects and the failure pattern when it does not, and the four ideas that run through all parts.

Stressor analysis, attractors and residues; the three rates of change (contracts and identifiers, engines, content); portability of listing data and events; the centralization pendulum and the cost to reverse; technical debt as a liquidity tax; the twelve marketplace fitness functions; the architecture function's own evolution.
believe: A target state assumes a known future; a marketplace group should design against stressors instead.
What lasts a decade is a few contracts, identifiers and measures, and a group should steer by fitness functions tied to matches rather than by program milestones.
can_do: Run a stressor analysis on a marketplace group and rank components by the residues they carry.
Estimate what a carve-out of one brand would cost and which residues would shorten it.
Define marketplace fitness functions with owners, counter-metrics and drills.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a ten-year platform plan, the reader replaces its target state with a stressor analysis and a fitness scorecard and says where long-term investment belongs.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A marketplace group presents a ten-year target-state diagram with one shared product platform for all brands, tracked by program milestones. Its owner may sell a brand within three years, a new platform law is expected, and a fifth of one brand's search traffic may soon arrive through an AI assistant. Using only this chapter: what do you put in place of the plan, and where should the long-term investment go?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A stressor analysis (capital, regulation, channel, supply, adversarial, supplier and physical-world stressors and their combinations) that finds the residues needed to survive them; investment in the top layer that survives most stressors (the listing event contract, stable identifiers, identity with pairwise identifiers, tenant-partitioned data, governed metrics), with engines chosen for replaceability and content changed as data; the cost to reverse written into each sharing decision, so product platforms are shared last; a separability estimate and a yearly tenant-exit tabletop; and a dozen fitness functions, each with an owner, a counter-metric and a failure pattern, with drills for rebuild and separability, reviewed quarterly instead of milestones.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Three moves: the book's argument restated (a liquidity machine), stressor analysis adapted from residuality theory, and marketplace fitness functions; then what lasts and what gets replaced, portability, the centralization pendulum, debt and the architecture function; evidence from the documented reversals of marketplace groups (Schibsted, Adevinta, Prosus, Zillow) and the fictional Veldmark's stressor workshop and scorecard; a hand-off to the cases of Part IX.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

The chapter's final section performs the journal's closing: it synthesizes the parts as stages of the liquidity machine, restates the introduction's central claim, and returns to the introduction's opening question of why a site whose every team reports green loses contacts per listing to a smaller competitor.

thesis.question: How does a Chief Architect keep a marketplace platform coherent over ten years of acquisitions, verticals, regulations and technology shifts?
thesis.claim: Over a decade a Chief Architect should not steer toward a target state. Instead: write down the argument the platform serves (turning fresh, trustworthy supply into matches, cell by cell, at a cost the business can carry); run a stressor analysis every year and after every capital event to find the few structures that survive many stressors (the listing event contract, stable identifiers, identity with pairwise identifiers, tenant-partitioned data) and spend design attention there, choosing engines for replaceability and changing content as data; write the cost to reverse into every sharing decision, so that moving a capability between central and local control is a costed, reversible decision rather than a reorganization; and steer by about a dozen marketplace fitness functions, each with an owner, a counter-metric and the failure pattern it guards against, with drills for rebuild and separability, reviewed every quarter in place of program milestones.
thesis.disputed_by: The standard architecture-program practice of drawing a ten-year target-state diagram, executing it as a program with milestones, fixing once what is central and what is local, and reporting progress by milestones delivered, listings and visits.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this owns the argument and the top layer of contracts and identifiers and leaves engines to platform teams and content to brands; keeps the stressor table in the architecture repository and re-runs it after every change of owner, portfolio or law; makes separability a review criterion like security, proved by a yearly tenant-exit tabletop; and shows the board the stressor table and the separability estimate once a year and the fitness scorecard every quarter.
thesis.how_why: Between 2016 and 2026 Schibsted pitched one global product and tech organization, demerged Adevinta, which bought eBay Classifieds Group, set out to converge two of its largest platforms, was taken private and moved to a decentralized, standalone model; Prosus exited OLX Autos and Zillow closed Zillow Offers. None had the decade it planned. At Veldmark's November 2027 stressor workshop, 11 of 14 stressors touched the listing event contract and core, 8 identity, 8 the data platform and 2 the media service; a combined scenario of selling Hearthly Spain amid a generated-photo fraud ring found one missing residue, source-tenant provenance on the shared block list. With the separability residues, a 2030 Hearthly carve-out needs transitional services for seven capabilities for about nine to twelve months; without them, an estimated twenty months or more. The advice forum adopted a twelve-function fitness scorecard on 8 December 2027.

role.contribution: Restates the book's argument as the liquidity machine, turns it into a stressor analysis and a fitness scorecard for steering the platform over a decade, closes Part VIII and carries the journal's closing, handing off to Part IX as evidence.

transition_in.carries_over: Ai-in-listing-systems' closing: AI is safe where the marketplace's structures are clean and accelerates the mess where they are not, and it is only one of the stressors a platform must absorb, alongside acquisitions, regulation and the swing between central and local control; with it, the decisions of the four earlier chapters.
transition_in.introduces: The book's argument restated in one page, stressor analysis and residues, what lasts and what gets replaced, and the marketplace fitness functions.

parts.title: Part IX — PRACTICE: How Others Built It

know: The dated public record of six cases: Adevinta's swing from federation (2019) through product convergence (2023) to standalone marketplaces (2025); OLX's shrinking from 45 markets (2018) to seven (year to March 2026) and its exit from OLX Autos; eBay Classifieds Group's thin shared layer and its 2020–2021 sale; AVIV's acquired portals, seller funnel and 2025 turn to local autonomy; the property portals' units of charge, licensed supply and Zillow Offers (February to November 2021); and the automotive leaders' published dealer contracts and price ratings.

The three kinds of statement the cases keep apart (documented fact with source and year, the author's reading, labeled reference-architecture inference) and, for each case, where the public evidence stops.
believe: The public record supports sharing the uniform layers and treats product convergence as a separate, riskier bet; it does not show a completed product-platform convergence in any case.
Separability is a design requirement for any shared capability in a group whose owner may sell, not a contingency plan.
A pattern the record only fails to contradict is not thereby supported, and the depth of a lesson follows the depth of the evidence.
can_do: Say, for each of the book's main patterns, whether the public record supports it, only fails to contradict it, or is silent.

Bring the case that fits a decision in front of them (a convergence plan, a possible sale, an adjacent bet, a valuation model moving to commit, a dealer-feed contract) and the decision rule its record gives.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one case, and every case supports at least one.
Each case's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
A reader who has read only Part IX can match five group decisions to the case whose record speaks to each and state what that record shows, with its date.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A marketplace group is weighing five proposals: merge its two largest generalist platforms into one product platform; prepare a brand for a possible sale within two years; launch an inventory-owning car business beside its listings; turn its property valuation model into cash offers to homeowners; and show dealers how a price change moves their car's price band and search position. Using only Part IX, which case speaks to each, and what does its record show?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Adevinta for the merger: the 2023 decision to make the leboncoin and Kleinanzeigen platforms 'a unified global platform', last reported 'progressing well' in May 2024 and followed by the 2025 decentralization, with no public source showing it completed; convergence needs its own investment case. eBay Classifieds (and Adevinta's 2025 break-up) for the sale: the UK regulator's 2021 remedy required transitional services for Gumtree UK's buyer, so keep a dependency register per brand and interfaces a third party could operate. OLX (and the automotive case's CarOffer) for the inventory business: OLX Autos reached US$1.6 billion of revenue in the year to March 2022 while losing money and was exited from 2023; build adjacent bets to be switched off. Property portals for the cash offers: Zillow made the Zestimate an initial cash offer in February 2021 and wound Zillow Offers down in November 2021; govern models by the decision they drive. Automotive for the price planner: mobile.de, CarGurus and Autotrader publish five-band price ratings, and a rating that feeds ranking and dealer tools shapes the prices it learns from, so govern it as a ranking model.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The last section of case-automotive (or a closing passage after it) performs the part's closing: it says what the six cases show together that no single case shows, why that matters for a group's platform decisions, and returns to the part introduction's test of which patterns the record supports, which it only fails to contradict, and where it is silent.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Does the end of case-automotive state something about Part IX as a whole that no single case states, say why it matters, and return to the part introduction's closing test?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A synthesis that the six verdict tables sort the book's patterns into supported (shared uniform layers, contracts at the supply boundary, rebuildable read models, model governance by decision tier), not contradicted, and silent (product internals across brands after 2024); a so-what that a group should share layers, design every shared capability to be separable and keep the vertical lessons in contracts and governed models; an explicit return to the part introduction's three-way test.

thesis.question: Do the book's patterns hold against what publicly documented marketplace groups actually did, and where does the public evidence stop?
thesis.claim: The dated public record of six cases (Adevinta, OLX Group, eBay Classifieds Group, AVIV Group, the property portals and the automotive marketplaces) supports the book's sharing pattern and contradicts none of its main claims, but only up to the product layer. Groups that shared the uniform, expensive layers (infrastructure, data, experimentation and narrow machine-learning services) documented voluntary adoption and consolidated tooling, while the two product-platform integrations announced (AVIV in 2021, Adevinta in 2023) gave way to local autonomy in 2025 with no public source showing either completed. Every change of owner turned shared dependencies into transitional services or separation costs, in proportion to how informal their interfaces were, and every inventory-owning adjacent bet in the record was exited, and the portfolio, not the platform strategy, decided how many markets a shared platform served, while the listing stacks that lasted were evolved in place rather than replaced; separability and switch-off therefore belong in the design. In the verticals, what transfers is published supply contracts, license terms carried as data, a shared boundary that stops short of the agent, and models governed by the decision they drive; and no case documents how any group runs search, ranking or listing services across brands.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that real groups' histories teach little about architecture, because each turn was a capital or market decision; or the reading that the 2025 reversals prove centralization wrong and a group should keep each marketplace fully independent; or the conviction that one shared product platform remains the end state a group should reach and the reversals were interruptions by new owners.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this cites the record only at the strength it has: shares infrastructure, data, experimentation and narrow ML services without hesitation; makes any product-platform convergence a separate investment case with scope, stage gates and an exit criterion per stage; reviews every shared capability for separability as if a tenant will leave within eighteen months; builds adjacent transactional or inventory businesses so that a retreat is a configuration change; publishes supply contracts and registers every model by the decision it drives; and treats the book's product-layer patterns as untested by the public record rather than proven.
thesis.how_why: The six cases were chosen because they bought, merged, shared, sold and retreated in public. Adevinta's shared Kubernetes platform grew from about 1,500 to more than 4,000 developers without a documented mandate, and ten experimentation tools became one; its 2023 convergence was last reported 'progressing well' in May 2024 before the 2025 move to 'a decentralised, standalone operating model' and the sale of Spain. AVIV's 2021 goal of 'a European real estate marketplace' became, by December 2025, local autonomy with group functions 'where they create clear advantages'. The UK regulator's 2021 remedy wrote transitional services for Gumtree UK into eBay's sale; OLX went from 45 markets (2018) to seven (year to March 2026), each exit taking its stack, and exited OLX Autos from 2023; CarGurus wound down CarOffer. Zillow turned the Zestimate into a cash offer in February 2021 and wound Zillow Offers down that November; Rightmove and mobile.de publish feed contracts with idempotency and reconciliation. AVIV publishes no engineering material, and no case documents a group's cross-brand product internals after 2024.

supporting_claims.claim: Sharing the uniform, expensive layers (infrastructure, data, experimentation, narrow machine-learning services), grown by voluntary adoption and coordinated by agreement, is where the record documents gains in adoption and consolidated tooling; converging whole product platforms is a separate and riskier bet, announced by Adevinta (2023) and AVIV (2021) and given up for local autonomy in 2025 with no public source showing it completed.

Every shared dependency must survive a change of owner: eBay's 2020–2021 sale, Adevinta's 2025 break-up and AVIV's 2025 carve-out turned shared platforms into transitional services, localized intellectual property and separation costs, and the interface type (agreement, external provider, published contract or undocumented parent dependency) predicted the cost.

The portfolio, not the platform strategy, decides how many markets a shared platform serves, and adjacent inventory and transactional bets should be built to be switched off: OLX shrank from 45 markets to seven and exited OLX Autos, CarGurus wound down CarOffer and Zillow wound down Zillow Offers, while the listing stacks that lasted were evolved in place rather than replaced.

In the verticals the lessons sit in contracts and governed models, not in shared products: property supply is licensed and its terms must travel as data, dealer-fed supply runs on published contracts and change feeds, a real-estate group's shared boundary stops short of the agent, and a model moved from informing to committing money or exposure (Zillow Offers, price ratings that feed ranking) needs the governance of its new decision.

The public evidence stops at the product layer and is uneven between cases: no case documents how a group runs search, ranking or listing services across its brands after 2024, and AVIV publishes no engineering material at all; so each case dates every fact, labels every inference and says where its record ends, and a book pattern the record only fails to contradict is reported as untested, not as supported.

role.contribution: Tests the book's patterns against real groups' documented history, separating dated fact from interpretation and saying where the evidence stops.

additional_patterns.applies_to: case-adevinta to case-ebay-classifieds (multi-country generalist groups), case-aviv to case-property-portals (real estate), case-automotive (automotive)

flow.rationale: The cases move from a whole group's platform strategy to one vertical's contracts and models. Adevinta comes first because it ran the full centralize-and-decentralize cycle in public and sets the three questions every later case asks (what was shared, at which layer, what it cost when the strategy changed); placed later, its layer map and its 2019 'large investment, uniform technology' test, which OLX, eBay and AVIV are measured against, would arrive after them. OLX follows because it answers the question Adevinta leaves open, what happens when the portfolio rather than the platform strategy changes; placed after eBay Classifieds, it would separate the two halves of the 2021 deal (Adevinta as buyer, eCG as seller) by a case about neither, and placed first it would open Part IX with portfolio exits before the reader has seen what a group shares and at which layer. eBay Classifieds follows both because it is Adevinta's 2021 acquisition seen from the seller's side: the chapter links to case-adevinta for everything after 2021 instead of retelling it, so placed before Adevinta it would point forward to the story it depends on. AVIV opens the real-estate pair by asking how much of a property portal a group can share across countries; case-property-portals opens with 'the question underneath it', what licensed supply, durable properties and valuation models demand of one portal, so the two cannot swap without the portals case losing its premise. opening.bridge: From Veldmark, a fictional group whose decisions show how the argument plays out but not that it is right, to groups that bought, merged, shared, sold and retreated in public, read under stricter evidence rules: documented fact with its source and year, the author's reading, and labeled reference-architecture inference.
opening.roadmap: Six cases in reading order (Adevinta, OLX Group, eBay Classifieds Group, AVIV Group, the property portals Zillow, Rightmove, Idealista and REA, and the automotive marketplaces mobile.de, Auto Trader and AutoScout24), each asking what was shared, at which layer and what it cost when the strategy changed, each ending with a verdict table and a comparison with Veldmark; a side-by-side table of the six; ending on the test that the reader can say which of the book's patterns the public record supports, which it only fails to contradict, and where it is silent.

closing.callback: The part introduction's closing test: which of the book's patterns the public record supports, which it only fails to contradict, and where it is silent.

takeaway.content: Use the toolkit's templates (the feed contract, the listing event specification, the entitlement matrix, the consolidation decision card) to put the record's lessons into the group's own decisions, and date every external fact cited in them.

thesis.question: What did Adevinta share across its marketplaces in each phase from the 2019 demerger to the 2025–2026 break-up, at which layer, and what did the sharing cost when its capital strategy changed?
thesis.claim: Adevinta's record supports deciding what to share by layer: its 2019 test, centralize where 'investment requirements are large and the technology is uniform', put infrastructure, data, experimentation and narrow machine-learning services on shared platforms that grew by voluntary adoption, whereas its 2023 decision to turn the leboncoin and Kleinanzeigen platforms into 'a unified global platform' was last reported 'progressing well' in May 2024 and then overtaken by the 2025 move to standalone marketplaces, in which central functions were ramped down, intellectual property was localized and central and local services ran in parallel. Since the record never reports the convergence completed or its savings realized, product-platform convergence needs its own investment case with scope and stage gates; and since a change of owner forced that unwinding, every shared capability must be designed to be separable.
thesis.disputed_by: The reading that Adevinta's 2025 reversal shows central platforms were a mistake and a group should keep its marketplaces independent; or the opposite reading that the convergence was sound and only the new owners interrupted it, so a group should still aim at one product platform for its generalist marketplaces.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect writes the two-part test into the group's architecture principles and makes every proposal for a shared capability answer both halves; measures a platform by how many tenants choose it and funds migration engineers rather than deadlines; requires any product-platform convergence to state its capabilities, markets, stage gates and exit criteria before it is staffed; and reviews every shared capability for separability (one account boundary per tenant, tenant-scoped data with contracts, deployment that runs outside the platform, clear ownership of code and models).
thesis.how_why: Demerged from Schibsted in April 2019 as a federation of locally built sites, Adevinta adopted a 'centralised strategy to data and analytics' while keeping product autonomy; its Common Platform served about 1,500 engineers in January 2020 and, as SCHIP, more than 4,000 developers in June 2023, with no mandate in the record. It bought eBay Classifieds Group in June 2021, targeting €130–165 million of run-rate cost synergies, and moved most EU5 platforms to AWS in 2023. The convergence decision came the same year; the take-private settled in May 2024; from July 2024 a new operating model 'empowering local marketplaces' ramped down central functions, localized intellectual property and ran central and local services in parallel, and Adevinta Spain was sold to EQT (announced July 2025, completed February 2026). The case is strongest on infrastructure and weakest exactly where the convergence bet was placed, so its completion cannot be judged from the public record.

role.contribution: The fullest public test of the centralization pendulum: what sharing by layer delivered, what product convergence left unproven, and what a change of owner made shared platforms cost.

thesis.question: What happened to OLX Group's listing platform as its portfolio shrank from 45 markets to seven and its adjacent businesses were exited, and what did its engineers change in the listing stack meanwhile?
thesis.claim: OLX's record shows that the portfolio, not the platform strategy, set what its shared platform was worth: every market it left between 2018 (45 markets) and its year to March 2026 (seven) took its stack with it, and its inventory and transactional bets, led by OLX Autos, were exited or de-prioritized; meanwhile the listing stack improved by evolution in place, with Solr and BM25 kept, ranking moved into the engine, paid visibility given its own objective and vector retrieval added as a fixed quota proved first in a smaller market's fallback path; so a group should fund shared capabilities for the markets it will keep, build adjacent businesses to be switched off, and change search through a proof sequence rather than a replacement.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that breadth across many markets is what makes a group's shared platform pay; that a classifieds group should move into owning inventory and handling transactions to capture more of each sale; and that adding vector search or modern ranking requires replacing the incumbent search engine.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect asks which markets will still be in the group in five years before funding a shared capability, and designs it so the others can leave; keeps an adjacent business's money with a licensed provider, its inventory systems outside the listing core and its entry points behind per-category flags; adopts OLX's hybrid-search proof sequence as a standard; makes paid visibility a named objective with an owner and puts a revenue guardrail next to the relevance metric of every ranking or retrieval change; and starts consolidation with identity and service-estate hygiene, measured in services migrated.
thesis.how_why: OLX rolled up and rebranded local sites across four continents, merged regional businesses into joint ventures, sold Avito in 2022 and left markets through sales, mergers and joint ventures. OLX Autos reached US$1.6 billion of revenue in the year to March 2022, just over half of the classifieds business, while losing money, and Prosus exited it from 2023; pay-and-ship was de-prioritized in Europe and the credit broker and services marketplace were sold. By the year to March 2026 OLX was seven markets with US$992 million of revenue, a 48% adjusted EBITDA margin and 71% of revenue from motors, real estate and jobs. Through all of it the engineering blog documents search moving from sort to formula to learning to rank in Solr, a separate 'VAS LTR' objective for paid visibility, and hybrid retrieval rolled out in a fixed sequence after it was found to penalize paid listings; multi-brand work moved to one front-end repository for three brands and one learning-to-rank repository with per-brand configuration.

role.contribution: Shows the portfolio, not the platform strategy, changing what a shared platform is worth, adjacent bets retired, and a listing stack evolved in place while the group around it shrank.

posts.title: eBay Classifieds Group: Shared Platforms, Local Brands and a Sale
posts.question: How thin a shared layer did eBay Classifieds Group run beneath its national brands, through which kinds of interface, and what did the 2020–2021 sale expose about that coupling?

A group should share the professional supply side of verticals before consumer products.

Classify a group's shared capabilities by interface type and say which would need transitional services in a sale.

The UK regulator's 2021 decision required eBay to offer transitional services to Gumtree UK's buyer, Adevinta promised to support the Australian businesses 'during the transition', and several brands were sold again within 18 months. thesis.question: How much of a property portal can a group share across countries, as AVIV's acquisitions, 2021 integration intent and 2025 turn to local autonomy show it from the outside?
thesis.claim: AVIV's documented integration moves were commercial and data-driven, not a shared listing platform: it shared valuation science and a bundled professional offer to capture sellers early and route them to paying agents, and its 2021 goal of 'a European real estate marketplace', never scoped in public, gave way by December 2025 to local autonomy with group functions 'where they create clear advantages'; the record therefore places a property group's shared boundary at infrastructure, data, engines and methods, short of the professional edge where national feed formats, disclosure rules, agent software and pricing norms meet, and it shows that an integration goal without a written scope cannot be changed cheaply.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that national property portals are similar enough (listings, search, agents, leads) for a group to run them on one European product platform, and that AVIV's 2025 reversal reflects its new owners' preferences rather than the vertical's limits.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect of a multi-country property group shares infrastructure, data, identity tooling and engines without hesitation, shares valuation and ranking methods as group science, and keeps feed adapters, disclosure validation, professional products and lead routing local; requires a layer-by-layer scope, markets per stage and an exit criterion per stage before staffing any integration goal; governs valuation as a supply product with an owner and published accuracy definitions; and builds the attribution chain behind commission-share revenue as local, consented and auditable work.
thesis.how_why: Axel Springer bought SeLoger (2010), 80% of Immoweb (2012), Immowelt combined with Immonet (2015, cleared by the Bundeskartellamt as Germany's second and third portals) and Logic-Immo (cleared in 2018), with Yad2 and Meilleurs Agents (bought for €200 million in September 2019 to 'widen the value chain'). Its integration moves were Ultimmo, one professional offer across SeLoger, Logic-Immo and Meilleurs Agents (November 2022), the 2023 opening of SeLoger to private sellers and seller leads monetized through commission share; Immowelt and Immonet still ran side by side nine years after combining. The 2021 CEO statement and the 2025 interview are the only public statements of intent and outcome; the phrase 'fully integrated platform' is the interviewer's. The carve-out became effective in April 2025 and a sale of Yad2 was signed in December 2025. AVIV publishes no engineering material, so the boundary is traced from strategy, not systems.

role.contribution: Traces from the outside where a property group's shared boundary sits, and shows an integration goal of unpublished scope giving way to local autonomy.

transition_in.carries_over: eBay Classifieds' closing: a federation whose value lay in strong national platforms and whose shared layer was tested by a sale.
transition_in.introduces: One vertical, real estate, and a group that took the opposite route: it assembled national portals by acquisition and set out to make them work as one, with almost no engineering evidence to read.

posts.title: Zillow, Rightmove, Idealista and REA: What Property Portals Teach
posts.question: What do licensed supply, durable properties, valuation models and the unit of charge demand of a property portal's architecture, as Zillow, Rightmove, REA and Idealista document them, and where does their evidence stop?

know: Zillow Offers in Zillow's own words: the Zestimate made an initial cash offer in 23 markets in February 2021, and the November 2021 wind-down after it was 'unable to accurately forecast future home prices at different times in both directions'.

Four economic engines: Rightmove per advertiser (£1,621 a month on average in 2025), REA per listing through vendor-paid depth, Zillow per lead through share of voice or a fee at closing; and why values across these rows cannot be compared.

Supply licensed from MLSs and agents (Zillow's data licenses that may restrict 'the training of models', its 2025 listing policy, lawsuit and March 2026 change), Rightmove's published feed contract, Idealista's duplicate clustering, and how little is public about REA's and Idealista's engineering.
believe: A model's governance follows the decision it drives, and moving it from informing to committing money is a governance event.
License terms, embargoes and agent relations belong in the architecture as data and controls.
can_do: Name the questions a commit-tier use of a valuation model must answer that a present-value back-test does not.
Choose the monetization core (contracts and quotas, per-listing orders, lead routing with attribution) for a portal's unit of charge.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a proposal to turn a portal's valuation estimate into cash offers, the reader uses Zillow's dated record to say what changes and which questions must be answered before launch.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A property portal's estimate has a low median error on homes currently listed. Its product team proposes offering homeowners cash at 94% of the estimate and reselling the homes. Using only this chapter: what does Zillow's record show, what changes about the model, and what must be answered before launch?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Zillow made the Zestimate an initial cash offer in 23 markets in February 2021 and in November 2021 was winding Zillow Offers down, 'unable to accurately forecast future home prices at different times in both directions'. The model is moved from describing present values (inform tier) to pricing purchases resold months later (commit tier), which needs a decision record signed outside the model team and its own validation: the price after the holding period, the error on the owners who would accept the offer (selection), and a capital limit on how many homes can be carried. The on-market error says little about off-market error.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's questions, its evidence and where it ends.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what questions will this chapter ask, what kind of evidence will it use, and how will it end?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Three properties of property portals (supply from an external system of record, the property as a durable entity, data that tempts the portal up the value chain) tested against decision tiers, the property model and feed contracts; four portals read for what each charges for, where its supply comes from, what its models may decide and what it published about its systems; evidence that is uneven (Zillow and Rightmove detailed, REA financial only, Idealista very little), with section depth following the evidence; a comparison with Veldmark's Hearthly.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

Every statement about Zillow, Rightmove, REA or Idealista's internal systems that no cited source documents sits in a callout or figure caption labeled as inference, and every company fact outside those labels carries its source and publication year.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Is there any sentence outside an `INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED` callout or a labeled figure caption that describes how Zillow, Rightmove, REA or Idealista builds or runs a system without a dated source, or a company fact with no source and year?
acceptance_criteria.expected: None. Undocumented internals appear only in labeled inference callouts or captions; each company fact names its source and year in the sentence or the timeline; the author's interpretation is marked 'my reading' or sits in the Chief Architect's view.

thesis.question: What do licensed supply, durable properties, valuation models and the unit of charge demand of a property portal's architecture, as Zillow, Rightmove, REA and Idealista document them, and where does their evidence stop?
thesis.claim: The property portals' record shows that what a portal's models may decide, where its supply comes from, what its durable entity is and what it charges for shape its architecture more than its technology choices do: Zillow moved the Zestimate from informing to committing capital in February 2021 and wound Zillow Offers down that November with no visible validation for the new use, so models must be governed by the decision they drive; supply is licensed from MLSs and agents who also feed rivals, so license, embargo and training terms must travel with every listing as data; a home is listed, sold, let and valued many times, so the property, not the listing, must be the durable entity that valuations, price history and duplicate clusters hang off; and Rightmove's per-advertiser, REA's per-listing and Zillow's per-lead charging each need a different monetization core. The evidence stops at REA's engineering and almost everything technical about Idealista.
thesis.disputed_by: The technology-first view that a portal's architecture is mainly its search, data and cloud stack; with it, the views that a valuation model good enough to show homeowners is good enough to price purchases, that data licenses and agent relations are contract matters for the legal and sales teams rather than architecture, that the listing is the natural unit of a portal's data, and that one monetization platform fits any portal whatever it charges for.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect registers models by the decision they drive and blocks a launch that changes a model's tier without a decision record signed outside the model team; carries each listing's license, embargo, attribution and training-eligibility terms from ingestion to search, syndication, AI-assistant feeds and training pipelines; designs the catalog and entitlement core so that listing-level orders and lead-level attribution are possible; makes the property, not the listing, the durable entity; and measures AI assistants as a lead channel by experiment on leads.
thesis.how_why: Zillow made the Zestimate an initial cash offer in 23 markets in February 2021 and in November 2021 was winding Zillow Offers down, writing that it had been 'unable to accurately forecast future home prices at different times in both directions'; the model had not got worse, it had been moved from describing present values to pricing purchases resold months later. Zillow's 10-K warns that MLS and data licenses may restrict 'the training of models', and its 2025 listing policy started a lawsuit before it changed the policy in March 2026. Rightmove charged £1,621 per advertiser a month on average in 2025 and publishes a feed contract with an idempotency key and snapshot reconciliation for lost deletes; REA sells vendor-paid depth per listing; Zillow charges per lead, with attribution over up to two years; Zillow's living database, REA's 5.2 million owner-tracked properties and Idealista's 2021 duplicate-control tool, which clusters listings of one home rather than deleting them, are all property-first assets. REA's engineering and nearly everything technical about Idealista are not public.

role.contribution: Shows the vertical lessons of real estate in the public record: model governance by decision tier, licensed supply carried as data, and the unit of charge shaping the monetization core.

transition_in.carries_over: AVIV's closing: how little of a property portal travels across borders, seen from the outside.
transition_in.introduces: The question underneath AVIV's: what licensed supply, durable properties and valuation models demand of one portal, read through the portals that publish the most about their economics and engineering.

posts.title: mobile.de, Auto Trader and AutoScout24: Lessons from Automotive Marketplaces
posts.question: What do the automotive leaders' published dealer contracts, investor reports and engineering posts reveal about a dealer-fed listing system, and where does the marketplace's responsibility end?

know: Why automotive behaves differently: a car carries a machine-readable identity, most cars are listed by dealers through software, and the dealer who supplies the stock is also the paying customer.

mobile.de's architecture as written in its APIs (transfer service providers as integration principals, idempotent creates, one write at a time per ad, taxonomy keyed to a vehicle derivative, the price rating as a resource, a change feed with a 24-hour catch-up window); Autotrader UK's disclosed levers, data APIs and Deal Builder; AutoScout24's platform story; CarGurus' price transparency and the CarOffer wind-down; OLX Autos as the contrast.

Price evaluation as a control loop across the cases (five-band ratings, no-rating paths, dealer tools that show how a price change moves the band or the search position) and where the evidence stops (mobile.de internals, AutoScout24's product platform, all valuation methods).
believe: In automotive the published dealer contract is the architecture document.

A price rating that feeds ranking or dealer tools needs the governance of a ranking model, and platform-controlled states on a dealer's stock are commercial-model changes that must be opt-in and reversible.
can_do: Write the commitments of a professional supply contract (accountable integrators, idempotent creates, one writer per listing, stable error keys, a change feed with replay, a notice period).
Decide how far up the transaction ladder a marketplace should go and what evidence would justify each step.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a motors marketplace planning a dealer price tool and online reservations, the reader uses the dated automotive record to say what each requires.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A motors marketplace that rates every car's price in five bands plans a dealer tool showing how a price cut would move the band and the car's search position, and wants to switch on online reservations for all dealers' stock. Using only this chapter: what does the public record show, and what should the marketplace put in place for each?
acceptance_criteria.expected: mobile.de, CarGurus and Autotrader publish five-band price ratings, and mobile.de shows dealers how a price change moves search position; once a rating feeds ranking and dealer tools the model shapes the prices it learns from, so it needs an owner, evaluation on band accuracy and boundary clustering, a no-rating path and ranking-change review. Autotrader's Deal Builder reached 137,000 full reservations in a year while forecourts fell in the second half and dealers cut paid stock, and its auto-rollout was paused for 'request a reservation'; reservations must be opt-in, configurable per dealer and reversible. Owning cars is a different business, from which CarGurus' CarOffer and OLX Autos retreated.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's questions, its evidence and where it ends.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what questions will this chapter ask, what kind of evidence will it use, and how will it end?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Three questions asked of each company (what the public contract reveals, what the reported numbers say about the systems behind them, where the marketplace's responsibility ends); evidence from integration API manuals, investor reports and engineering posts for mobile.de, Autotrader UK, AutoScout24 and CarGurus, with OLX Autos as the brief contrast; tests of feed contracts, change feeds and model governance; a comparison with Veldmark's Motorvane and the close of Part IX's cases.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

Every statement about mobile.de, Autotrader, AutoScout24 or CarGurus's internal systems that no cited source documents sits in a callout or figure caption labeled as inference, and every company fact outside those labels carries its source and publication year.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Is there any sentence outside an `INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED` callout or a labeled figure caption that describes how mobile.de, Autotrader, AutoScout24 or CarGurus builds or runs a system without a dated source, or a company fact with no source and year?
acceptance_criteria.expected: None. Undocumented internals appear only in labeled inference callouts or captions; each company fact names its source and year in the sentence or the timeline; the author's interpretation is marked 'my reading' or sits in the Chief Architect's view.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter's final section performs Part IX's closing: it says what the six cases show together that no single case shows, why it matters, and returns to the part introduction's test of which patterns the record supports, which it only fails to contradict, and where it is silent, before handing off to the toolkit.

thesis.question: What do the automotive leaders' published dealer contracts, investor reports and engineering posts reveal about a dealer-fed listing system, and where does the marketplace's responsibility end?
thesis.claim: Because a car has a machine-readable identity, arrives through dealer software and is supplied by the customer who pays, the automotive leaders' public record is their architecture: mobile.de's and Autotrader's published dealer contracts (accountable integrators, idempotent creates, serialized writes, a change feed with replay) are the documented answer to unmanaged feeds; their five-band price ratings, once shown to dealers alongside search position or used in ranking, shape the prices they learn from and need ranking-model governance; and the marketplace's responsibility ends where platform-controlled state on a dealer's stock stops being opt-in and reversible, as Deal Builder's friction and the CarOffer and OLX Autos retreats show.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a dealer feed is an import job each marketplace tunes privately, that a price rating is a neutral label rather than a model with consequences, and that a marketplace should move into reservations, guarantees and owning cars to capture more of each sale.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect publishes the professional supply contract before building the importer and treats vendor certification as a release gate; publishes change with a stated delay and replay window, 24 hours by default; registers any price rating that labels or orders results as a ranking model with an owner, band-boundary monitoring and a no-rating path; derives billing counts from the same inventory state search shows; makes every platform-set transactional state opt-in, configurable per dealer and reversible; and runs data APIs as a business line with their own service levels.
thesis.how_why: Nine-tenths of automotive supply arrives through dealer feeds. mobile.de's Seller API and Ad Stream document transfer service providers as integration principals, idempotent creates, one write at a time per ad, a taxonomy keyed to a vehicle derivative and a change feed with a 24-hour catch-up window, and its price planner links price to search position. mobile.de, CarGurus and Autotrader all publish five-band price ratings or flags. Autotrader UK discloses its levers, serves about 155 million data-API calls a month, and by March 2026 had more than 6,700 retailers on Deal Builder with 137,000 full reservations in the year, while forecourts fell in the second half and dealers cut paid stock. CarGurus' 2025 annual report records the wind-down of CarOffer, and Prosus exited OLX Autos from 2023. mobile.de's internals, AutoScout24's product platform and every valuation method remain unpublished.

role.contribution: Tests the supply contract, change feed and model-governance patterns in the vertical that publishes its contracts, marks where the marketplace's responsibility ends, and closes Part IX with the hand-off to the toolkit.

transition_in.carries_over: The property portals' closing: a listing business sitting on valuable data and a professional supply base it does not control.
transition_in.introduces: The same questions in a vertical where the durable entity is the vehicle, the professional is a dealer and supply is written by dealer software, not licensed from agents.

know: Where the book's twelve working templates, its definitions and its sources are, and how the three pages refer to each other and to the owning chapters.
can_do: Start from the decision on their desk and find the template to copy, the definition of each term it uses, and the dated sources behind the chapter that teaches it.
Weigh a claim in the book by the kind and age of the source behind it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is served by at least one reference page.
Each reference page's closing points the reader to the next page in the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
Using only the three reference pages, a reader goes from one decision to its template, the definitions of the template's key terms and the dated sources of the chapter behind it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your group is about to sign a new bulk-feed partner. Using only the Reference pages: which template do you copy, where do you find what 'full snapshot' and 'delta feed' mean and which chapter owns them, and how do you find the sources that chapter rests on and judge how current they are?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Tool 5, the feed contract, in the toolkit (found through its 'Find the Template for the Question on Your Desk' table), with its Veldmark example and the link to listing-ingestion; the glossary's Part III — Supply section, where full snapshot and delta feed are defined in adjacent rows with listing-ingestion as the owning chapter, or the alphabetical index; the bibliography's Sources by Chapter list for listing-ingestion, each entry giving its year and evidence type, read with the register's rule that company engineering evidence older than about three years records that date, not today.

thesis.question: In what form must the book's templates, definitions and sources be kept for a reader to reuse a decision record, settle what a term means and weigh the evidence behind a claim?
thesis.claim: A reader can reuse the book's decision records, settle what its terms mean and weigh its evidence only if the reference matter is kept as maintained records rather than an appendix: twelve templates that each name an owner, a stable identifier and the removal path, kept as data where the systems live and cited by identifier; one plain definition per term, set beside the terms it is confused with and linked to the one chapter that owns it; and one register of the 587 cited sources, each with its year, evidence type and citing chapters.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a book's reference matter is a convenience appendix (sample forms to fill in completely, an alphabetical word list, a reading list for completeness) that the reader can skip without losing anything the chapters say.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect copies one template for the decision in front of them and keeps it in the repository or service it describes, fills only the fields that change the decision and writes 'unknown' rather than guessing; treats a disagreement between a chapter and the glossary as a defect to fix; and checks the year and evidence type of a source before citing it in a decision record.
thesis.how_why: Seven of the twelve templates have a field for what happens when a listing ends, because ended listings that survive in unregistered copies (the book's Ghost Inventory pattern) are found only through that field; the records cite each other by identifier (`listing.events.v1`, `POL-FRAUD-PAYLINK` v3, `pro-150@v5`), which lets a reader follow a stale listing back to the contract that allowed it. When 'contact' means a message in one warehouse and a lead in another, numbers cannot be compared, so the glossary keeps one meaning and one owning chapter per term. The register was harvested from the Sources and Evidence sections of 55 pages and gives each source's evidence type because a company engineering post records one group's platform at one date, a filing reported numbers, a regulation a requirement.

supporting_claims.claim: The book's recurring decisions are kept as twelve small templates, each with an owner, a stable identifier, the removal behavior and dates, maintained as data where the systems live, citing each other by identifier and filled in once for Veldmark. A template copied into a slide deck, without owner or identifier, stops being true within a quarter and leaves an incident nothing to trace back to.

Each term has one plain-language definition, grouped by part beside the terms most often confused with it, linked to the chapter that owns it and indexed alphabetically, with regulatory and company terms dated as of 2026. Without one owned meaning per term, the same word ('contact', 'lead') counts different things in different systems and the group's numbers cannot be compared.

Every cited source appears once, with a stable identifier, its year, its evidence type and the pages that cite it, findable by topic and by chapter, so a claim can be weighed by the kind and age of its evidence. A source listed without its date and type would let an engineering post from one year stand for a system as it runs today.

role.contribution: Collects the instruments, vocabulary and evidence the parts rely on.

flow.rationale: The pages are lookups, and their order is set first by the hand-offs they already make: case-automotive ends by naming the toolkit and the templates its comparison used; the toolkit ends by pointing to the glossary for the terms its templates use and to the bibliography for the sources behind them; the glossary ends by pointing to both. That chain also runs from acting (a template), to reading (a definition), to checking (a source). Placed first, the bibliography would open the reference matter with 587 entries the reader has no task for, and the case chapter's hand-off to the toolkit would skip past it; a reader's understanding would survive any order, since every term the toolkit uses was introduced in the chapters, but those hand-offs would not.

hook.content: These are working templates for a group of listing marketplaces: the records that Parts I to VIII ask a Chief Architect to keep.

opening.bridge: From the decisions argued across the book and tested in Part IX's cases to the records a team keeps for them, each tested against Veldmark and kept as maintained data, not documents.
opening.roadmap: A table that finds the template for the question on the reader's desk, a diagram of how the records reference each other, the twelve tools in the order of the parts that teach them, and how to keep them true over time; then the glossary for the terms and the bibliography for the sources.

closing.synthesis: The three pages are one reference chain: a template's field names a term, the term's row names its owning chapter, and that chapter's identifiers in the register name the dated sources behind it.
closing.so_what: A reader can trace any decision record built from the book back through its definitions to evidence of a known kind and age, and see which parts rest on fiction (Veldmark) or labeled inference rather than on sources.
closing.callback: The toolkit's opening claim that each template leaves evidence someone else can check.

posts.title: Glossary: The Language of Listing Systems
posts.question: What does each of the book's terms mean, which terms is it most often confused with, and which chapter owns it?

know: Where each term is defined: the evidence labels and fifteen failure patterns, one section per part from I to VIII, the Veldmark names, and the alphabetical index of every term, abbreviation and alias.
can_do: Look up a term and read the neighboring rows that carry the contrasts behind real design errors (listing versus underlying entity, publication state versus enforcement overlay, full snapshot versus delta feed, contact versus conversation versus lead, entitlement versus effect, system of record versus read model).
Follow a term to its owning chapter, and check a regulatory or company term against its current source before using it in a contract or policy.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a pair of terms that are often confused, the reader finds both on the page, states the difference in their own words and names the owning chapter.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: what is the difference between a contact, a conversation and a lead, and between the publication state and the enforcement overlay of a listing? Which chapter owns each pair?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A contact is any action by which a buyer reaches a seller about a listing (a message, form, call, callback, booking or application); a conversation is the platform-held thread of messages about one listing; a lead is a record, created by a defined rule, that a specific buyer expressed interest in a professional's listing, delivered to that professional and tracked to an outcome (all messaging-and-leads). The publication state is owned by the listing (draft, active, sold, expired and so on); the enforcement overlay is owned by trust and safety (none, held, restricted, blocked, restored); visibility and contactability are derived from both (listing-aggregate).

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone can say how the page is organized and how to use it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: how is this page organized, and how should you use it?

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the page, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone can say what the register includes and excludes and how to use it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what does this register include and leave out, and how should you use it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Only sources a page actually cited, each once, with its year, evidence type and citing pages, findable by topic or chapter; research conducted in October 2026, some facts known through secondary summaries, names as of 2026; research briefs and Veldmark are not sources; weigh claims by the kind and age of the source.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the page, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

role.contribution: Gives every documented fact in the book a findable source of known kind and age, and performs the reference part's closing.

transition_in.carries_over: The glossary's closing pointer: the sources behind the definitions, with their evidence type and publication date, are listed by topic and chapter in the bibliography.
transition_in.introduces: The register of the public sources the pages cite, with the rules for weighing each by its kind and age.
